questions.stem: The phrase “fresh-feathered birds flitted with song” is an example of
questions.explain: The repeated ‘f’ sound in ‘fresh-feathered … flitted’ is alliteration. There is no comparison using ‘like’ or ‘as’, so it is not a simile, and no word imitates the sound it names, so it is not onomatopoeia.

questions.stem: The phrase “parrots squawking like matriarchal fishwives” is an example of which pair of literary devices?
questions.explain: The word ‘like’ makes it a simile, and comparing the birds to bossy market women gives them human qualities, which is personification. ‘Squawking’ suggests a sound, but the key effect is the comparison to people.

questions.stem: Which of the following would be an advantage if Haldane conducted interviews?
options: Considerable depth of the information to be collected
High reliability of the information to be collected
questions.explain: Interviews let the researcher probe and ask follow-up questions, so the information collected is detailed and in-depth. They are costly, reach few people, and their results are usually less reliable than those of a standard questionnaire.

questions.stem: Haldane found an article entitled “Modern Technology Causing Canadian Students to Fail”. This article could be useful to his research as it
questions.explain: The article reports someone else’s findings, so it is secondary data that Haldane can use as background. It is not primary data because he did not collect it, and we cannot assume it is reliable or sufficient for his own school.

questions.stem: Which of the following must the research company consider when selecting a sample?
options: How well it represents the population
questions.explain: A sample is useful only if it represents the population being studied, so that the findings can be applied to the whole group. The other options do not decide whether a sample is suitable.

questions.stem: Which of the following would be the MOST reliable source of secondary data for this study?
questions.explain: Attendance registers are official records kept every day, so they give an accurate account of who was absent and when. Letters from parents may be missing or untrue, and report cards only summarise attendance.

questions.stem: What feature of Caribbean English Creole grammar is used in the expression “Crosby ain’t tell him nothing”?
questions.explain: ‘Ain’t’ and ‘nothing’ are two negatives in the same clause, a Creole double negative used for emphasis. Standard English would say ‘Crosby didn’t tell him anything’. No word is repeated and no verb is missing.

questions.stem: What does the extract suggest about the relationship between the boy’s education and his use of language?
options: His education allows him to speak properly.
His education has influenced his language.
As an economist, he speaks Standard English.
He speaks English Creole because he is an educated lawyer.
questions.explain: Since going away to study, the boy says ‘Dad’ and ‘those thangs’, copying English speech, so his education has changed how he speaks. The narrator does not even know whether he is a lawyer or an economist, so C and D do not fit.

questions.stem: What is the speaker’s purpose for writing this letter?
options: To protest against police brutality and injustice
To apologize for being locked up along with Jim
To inform his mother of his current address and console her
To tell his mother that he and Jim are in jail and to explain why
questions.explain: Sonny writes ‘I don’t know how to tell yu dis’ and then explains how Jim was arrested and why he fought the police, so his purpose is to break the news and explain it. The poet may be protesting injustice, but Sonny is not.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a purpose for which the writer uses Caribbean English Creole in the poem?
options: To provide aesthetic pleasure to the reader
To serve as a vehicle of easy communication between inmates
To show that it is more suited than standard English to discuss the issues of racism and social injustice
To persuade the reader that the issues of racism and social injustice deserve discussion
questions.explain: The letter goes from Sonny to his mother, not between prisoners, so easy communication between inmates is not a purpose of the Creole. The poet uses it for its sound and rhythm and to give a powerful voice to the issue of injustice.

questions.stem: Based on the tone of the letter, the relationship between mother and son can be described as
questions.explain: Sonny keeps addressing ‘Mama’, hopes she is in good health and urges her, ‘don’t fret … Be of good courage’. This loving, caring tone shows an affectionate relationship. ‘Cordial’ means merely polite and friendly, which is too distant.

questions.stem: In which of the following countries is Sonny MOST likely incarcerated?
questions.explain: The letter is headed ‘Jebb Avenue, S.W. 2 Inglan’. ‘Inglan’ is the Creole pronunciation of England, and S.W. 2 is a London postal district. Sonny’s Jamaican Creole tells us where he comes from, not where he is held.

questions.stem: From Percy’s statements, what are the two varieties of language MOST likely spoken by Mavis’ grandchildren?
questions.explain: One grandchild ‘talk so nice, like the people in the television shows’, which suggests Standard English. The other keeps saying ‘I and I’, a feature of Rastafarian speech (Dread Talk). ‘Television English’ is not a recognised variety.

questions.stem: What does Percy’s statement “He should know that people don’t talk so in church” suggest?
options: Percy does not like Mavis’ grandson.
Context is critical to the choice of code.
There is a code reserved only for church.
questions.explain: Percy means that a church funeral calls for a particular kind of language, so the grandson should have matched his code to the setting. That is the idea that context guides the choice of code, not that a special church-only language exists.

questions.stem: Which of the following technologies would NOT help to enhance the delivery of the eulogy?
questions.explain: A microphone, music and projected slides can all support a speaker in front of a congregation. A fax machine sends documents to another place, so it adds nothing to a live speech.

questions.stem: An English Creole may be defined as a language
options: used by the poorest people in the society
only understood by some persons in the society
developed from contact between European languages and African languages
questions.explain: Caribbean English Creoles grew out of contact between English (a European language) and West African languages during slavery and colonisation. The other options repeat negative myths: Creoles are full languages used by people of every social group.

questions.stem: In which of the following expressions is the process of reduplication evident?
questions.explain: Reduplication repeats a word to change or intensify its meaning, so ‘chaka-chaka’ means very untidy or disorganised. ‘Eye-water’ (tears) and ‘step-sister’ join two different words, and ‘A waa gwaan’ is a greeting.

questions.stem: What kind of communication context is depicted in the conversation?
questions.explain: The cartoon shows two people talking face to face, so the context is interpersonal. The man’s ‘tch!’ thought bubble is intrapersonal, but the conversation as a whole is between the couple.

questions.stem: Which of the following features of non-verbal communication would candidates be LEAST likely to use when giving speeches?
options: Waving their hands in the air
Turning their backs to the audience
Smiling at the women in the audience
Embracing a spouse or other close family member
questions.explain: Candidates want to connect with voters, so they wave, smile and show family warmth. Turning their backs to the audience breaks eye contact and suggests rejection, so it would damage their message.

questions.stem: Which of the following verbal strategies would NOT help candidates to effectively get their message across?
questions.explain: Statistics, slogans and announcements give voters clear, memorable information. Sarcasm is easily misunderstood or taken as an insult, so it is more likely to turn voters away than to win their support.

questions.stem: The scene suggests that INAPPROPRIATE postings can be made by
options: the three characters in the cartoon
persons of different ages and genders
questions.explain: The cartoon shows a young man, a woman and an older man with glasses, all hurt by their posts. The artist uses this mix to suggest that anyone, of any age or gender, can post something inappropriate.

questions.stem: Which of the following could be considered the artist’s purpose for depicting the scene?
options: To show that social media are dangerous
To warn against indiscriminate use of social media
To ridicule persons addicted to using social media
To show that social media are a sign of the end times
questions.explain: The cartoon shows what can happen after careless posting, warning viewers to think before they post. It does not say that social media are dangerous in themselves, only that using them without care can be costly.

questions.stem: What method of data collection did the researcher use?
questions.explain: The researcher held a discussion with small sets of students who share the same experience, which is what a focus group is. An interview is usually one-to-one, and he did not join the classes as a participant observer.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an advantage of using a questionnaire for this particular study?
options: It has a low rate of response.
The researcher is able to ask follow-up questions.
Respondents don’t have to think carefully before formulating a response.
questions.explain: Questionnaires put the same, mostly closed questions to everyone, so the answers can easily be counted and turned into percentages. A low response rate is a disadvantage, and follow-up questions are a feature of interviews.

questions.stem: Which of the following would be the MOST appropriate population for this study?
options: All students of Argyle Secondary that have been attending classes irregularly
All senior students of Argyle Secondary that have been attending classes irregularly
All students of secondary students in the country that have been attending classes irregularly
All senior students of secondary students in the country that have been attending classes irregularly
questions.explain: The ministry is concerned about senior students at Argyle Secondary who attend irregularly, so that exact group is the population. Option A includes junior students, and options C and D go beyond the one school being investigated.

questions.stem: If the research company was observing the patterns of absenteeism among senior students, which of the following would be an advantage?
options: Directly experiencing the behaviour of participants
Allowing its biases to affect what is observed
Spending a long enough period of time collecting data
Participants changing their behaviour while being observed
questions.explain: Observation lets the researcher see behaviour first-hand instead of relying on what people say. Bias and participants changing their behaviour are disadvantages, and needing a long time in the field is a cost rather than a benefit.

questions.stem: Which feature of Caribbean English Creole grammar is used in the expression “Crosby ain’t tell him nothing”?
questions.explain: ‘Ain’t’ and ‘nothing’ are two negatives in the same clause, a Creole double negative used for emphasis. Standard English would say ‘Crosby didn’t tell him anything’. No word is repeated and no verb is missing.

questions.stem: What does the extract suggest about the relationship between the boy’s education and his use of language?
options: His education makes him speak properly.
His education has influenced his language.
As an economist, he speaks Standard English.
He speaks English Creole because he is an educated lawyer.
questions.explain: Since going away to study, the boy says ‘Dad’ and ‘those thangs’, copying English speech, so his education has changed how he speaks. The narrator does not even know whether he is a lawyer or an economist, so C and D do not fit.

questions.stem: Which of the following does NOT contribute to the tension among the characters?
options: Miss Clemmie looking at Ascot as if he is a stranger
Dagoman silently angry with Ascot for snapping at the children
Miss Clemmie feeling proud to have Ascot drive her in his car
questions.explain: Ascot snapping at the children, Miss Clemmie staring at him like a stranger and Dagoman’s silent anger all add to the bad feeling. Miss Clemmie’s pride in being driven by her son is a warm feeling, so it does not add to the tension.

questions.stem: The writer’s use of English Creole throughout the extract suggests all of the following EXCEPT that she
options: accepts that English Creole is a broken language
thinks that English Creole is an authentic language
thinks that English Creole can be used for literary purposes
accepts that English Creole is a means of communication by people
questions.explain: By telling the story in Creole, Senior treats it as an authentic, expressive language fit for literature and everyday communication. Calling it ‘broken English’ is a negative attitude that her choice of language rejects.

questions.stem:
Which of the following are non-standard English texts?
I. ‘what I’s got to sweat blood for’
II. ‘Three pence!’
III. ‘Did yo’ hear thet, Maud?’
questions.explain: ‘What I’s got’ uses ‘what’ for ‘that’ and a non-standard verb form, and ‘yo’’ and ‘thet’ show dialect pronunciation. ‘Three pence!’ is acceptable Standard English, so only I and III are non-standard.

questions.stem: Which of the following BEST explains the meaning of the term ‘lingua franca’?
options: A language which is derived from French and used by African slaves.
Any language which is native to African peoples who have been transplanted.
Any language which is foreign to a speaker who moves to a new speech community.
A language used as a common means of communication by speakers whose native languages are different.
questions.explain: A lingua franca is a shared language that lets people with different first languages communicate, as English does when delegates from Suriname, Haiti and Jamaica meet at CARICOM. Despite its name, it has nothing to do with French.

questions.stem: Which of the following contexts of communication BEST describes the interaction between the two groups of students?
questions.explain: Jamaican and Cuban students bring different languages and cultures to the exchange, so it is intercultural communication. The visitors may meet in small groups, but the key feature is the meeting of two cultures.

questions.stem: While in Cuba, the students attended a seminar. The guest speaker noticed that many of the visitors seemed restless during his presentation, even though he was speaking audibly. Which of the following was NOT likely responsible for their restlessness?
options: He was speaking in a monotone.
He was using many unfamiliar words.
He complemented his speech with projected slides.
questions.explain: Speaking too fast, in a flat monotone or with unfamiliar words makes a talk hard for visitors to follow. Projected slides support understanding, especially for listeners working in a second language, so they would not cause restlessness.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the stage of the communication process at which Sally generated ideas for her speech?
questions.explain: Conceptualising is the first stage, when the sender forms the ideas to be communicated. Decoding and interpreting are done by the receiver, and feedback is the receiver’s response.

questions.stem: Which of the following BEST explains why some students covered their mouths and glanced at one another?
options: They were angry at Sally’s choice of words.
They were amused by Sally’s choice of words.
questions.explain: Covering their mouths and snickering are signs of trying to hide laughter. The students were amused by Sally’s ‘Yeah, yeah!’ opening and her repetitive ‘My father black, my mother black’, not bored or angry.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a message that Sally’s lack of eye contact could be sending?
options: She did not do enough research.
questions.explain: A speaker whose eyes are ‘glued to the paper’ seems nervous, unsure of her material or unable to speak freely. A well-prepared speaker knows the content well enough to look at the audience, so lack of eye contact does not suggest good preparation.

questions.stem: If Barry had held up his hand and turned his palm towards his father when the latter asked his question, what communication function would he be engaging in?
questions.explain: A raised palm signals ‘wait’ or ‘stop’, controlling the flow of the conversation. Gestures that manage turn-taking in this way perform the regulating function of non-verbal communication.

questions.stem: Barry’s use of “cool” in Frame 5 is an example of
questions.explain: ‘Cool’ meaning good or fashionable is informal vocabulary popular with young people, which is slang. Jargon is the technical language of a profession, and a dialect is a whole variety of a language, not a single word.

questions.stem: A student’s expository essay should typically aim to
questions.explain: Exposition explains and informs, so its aim is to enlighten and instruct. Recounting experiences belongs to narrative, appealing to the emotions belongs to persuasion, and presenting a personal viewpoint belongs to argument.

questions.stem: Which of the following would be the MAIN organizational strategy used in an expository essay on the topic: “Types of luxury vehicles”?
questions.explain: The word ‘types’ signals classification: sorting luxury vehicles into groups and explaining each group. Description and comparison may appear within paragraphs, but the overall structure is built on categories.

questions.stem: Which of the following techniques is typically NOT used in exposition?
questions.explain: Exposition aims to inform objectively, so it relies on facts, statistics, expert information and supporting details. Emotive language is designed to stir the reader’s feelings and belongs to persuasive writing.

questions.stem: Which of the following would be an advantage if Haldane conducted interviews?
options: High reliability of the information to be collected
In-depth nature of the information to be collected
questions.explain: Interviews let the researcher probe and ask follow-up questions, so the information collected is detailed and in-depth. They are costly, reach few people, and their results are usually less reliable than those of a standard questionnaire.

questions.stem: Haldane found an article entitled “Modern Technology Causing Canadian Students to Fail”. This article could be useful to his research as it
questions.explain: The article reports someone else’s findings, so it is secondary data that Haldane can use as background. It is not primary data because he did not collect it, and we cannot assume it is reliable or sufficient for his own school.

questions.stem: Which of the following factors can invalidate the generalization which the researcher makes from the findings?
options: The sample size is too large.
The sample is not representative of the population.
The research is carried out only in Ms Davis’ school.
The research is conducted during end of year examination.
questions.explain: A generalisation is valid only if the sample represents the population. Ms Davis is studying her own school, so option C is not a problem, and a large sample makes findings stronger, not weaker.

questions.stem: The mode of writing that Ms Davis should employ in her report is
questions.explain: A research report explains findings and reasons objectively, which is exposition. It does not tell a story, try to persuade the reader, or mainly describe how things look.

questions.stem: What feature of Caribbean English Creole grammar is used in the expression “Crosby ain’t tell him nothing”?
questions.explain: ‘Ain’t’ and ‘nothing’ are two negatives in the same clause, a Creole double negative used for emphasis. Standard English would say ‘Crosby didn’t tell him anything’. No word is repeated and no verb is missing.

questions.stem: What does the extract suggest about the relationship between the boy’s education and his use of language?
options: His education has influenced his language.
His education hindered his use of Standard English.
He speaks English Creole because he is an educated lawyer.
His education has nothing to do with his use of Standard English.
questions.explain: Since going away to study, the boy says ‘Dad’ and ‘those thangs’, copying English speech, so his education has influenced his language. It has not hindered his Standard English, and he is not speaking Creole.

questions.stem:
Which of the following expressions contains features of non-standard English dialect?
I. “… you ain’t never did.”
II. “… what I’s got to sweat blood for …”
III. “… sat under the breadfruit tree …”
questions.explain: ‘Ain’t never did’ uses a double negative with a non-standard verb form, and ‘what I’s got’ uses ‘what’ for ‘that’ and ‘I’s’ for ‘I have’. ‘Sat under the breadfruit tree’ is Standard English, so only I and II qualify.

questions.stem: Which of the following registers is used in the dialogue?
questions.explain: The old man jokes with his wife in relaxed, non-standard speech, using a pet name (‘Maudie’). That everyday family talk is casual register, not the fixed wording of frozen register or the careful language of formal and consultative register.

questions.stem: An English Creole in the Caribbean may be defined as a language
options: used by the poorest people in the society
only understood by some persons in the society
developed from contact between Europeans and Africans
questions.explain: Caribbean English Creoles grew out of contact between English (a European language) and West African languages during slavery and colonisation. The other options repeat negative myths: Creoles are full languages used by people of every social group.

questions.stem: At which stage of the communication process did the students giggle?
questions.explain: The giggling is the audience’s response to the message, which is feedback. Encoding and conceptualisation are done by the speaker, and decoding happens before the listeners react.

questions.stem: Which of the following BEST explains why the student misunderstood the question?
options: She did not do enough research.
She is weak and did not ask questions.
She is incapable of using Standard English.
She misunderstood a key word in the topic.
questions.explain: In the topic, ‘favour’ means ‘prefer’, but the student took it to mean ‘look like’, as in ‘people say I look like my father’. Misreading this key word sent her whole speech off topic.

questions.stem: What kind of communication context is depicted in the conversation?
questions.explain: The cartoon shows two people talking face to face, so the context is interpersonal. The man’s ‘tch!’ thought bubble is intrapersonal, but the conversation as a whole is between the couple.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the result of the inappropriate use of social media by the characters?
options: Access by future employers to the Internet
questions.explain: The signs show that each character’s posts embarrassed them and cost them job chances, so their reputations have been damaged. Employers are not simply slow to respond; the characters call themselves unemployable.

questions.stem: The MAIN function of the first line of the advertisement is to
options: help the reader to lose weight
questions.explain: ‘Want to lose weight?’ is a hook: a direct question about the reader’s own concern that makes them stop and read. Encouraging a response comes later, with ‘Don’t wait!’ and ‘Use SLIMS’.

questions.stem:
You are asked to speak to a group of twenty kindergarten children on the topic of environmental cleanliness.
Which of the following would be the MOST appropriate way to share the information with your audience?
questions.explain: Young children respond best to lively, colourful material with a simple spoken explanation, so animation with speech suits them. A panel discussion, a documentary or text-heavy slides would be too formal to hold their attention.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the correct sequence that a presenter should follow to successfully complete the communication process?
options: Encoding the message, selecting the channel, selecting audience, disseminating the message
Encoding the message, transmitting the message, selecting channel, disseminating the message
Conceiving the message, encoding the message, selecting the channel, disseminating the message
Conceiving the message, interpreting the feedback, selecting audience, disseminating the message
questions.explain: The sender must first conceive the message, then encode it into words or images, choose a suitable channel and finally send it out. Options A and B skip the first stage, and D puts feedback before the message has even been sent.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a feature of exposition?
options: Use of facts and relevant statistics
questions.explain: Exposition aims to inform objectively, so it relies on facts, statistics, expert information and supporting details. Emotive language is designed to stir the reader’s feelings and belongs to persuasive writing.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the MOST appropriate method for collecting the data?
questions.explain: To find out which cars many people prefer, the class needs the same questions put to a large number of buyers, which a questionnaire does efficiently. A checklist (B) is tempting, but it records observations rather than people’s preferences.

questions.stem: Which of the following does NOT reflect how an interview might be administered for this research?
options: Sending an email to a manager
Talking with a contact over the phone
questions.explain: An interview means questioning a person, whether by email, by phone or face to face. Taking note of certified vehicles is observation or document study, not an interview, so it does NOT reflect how an interview is administered.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a reliable secondary source of data for the research?
questions.explain: Newspaper articles report information gathered by someone else, so they are a secondary source. Licensing officers, consumers and car sales managers (A, C, D) would be questioned directly, which makes them primary sources.

questions.stem: Which of the following must the research company consider when selecting a sample?
options: How well it represents the population
questions.explain: A sample must represent the population so that the findings can be applied to the whole group. Option D is tempting, but respondents are chosen for representativeness, not for how knowledgeable they are.

questions.stem: If the research company used observation as a method of collecting data, which of the following would be an advantage?
options: Predicting the behaviour to be observed
Directly witnessing the behaviour of participants
Spending an extended period of time collecting data
Participants changing their behaviour while being observed
questions.explain: The main advantage of observation is that the researcher sees the behaviour directly instead of relying on what people say. Option D is actually a weakness of observation, because people may act differently when watched.

questions.stem:
If the research company only collected data in the morning, which of the following would be adversely affected?
I. Validity
II. Time spent in the field
III. Access to informants
questions.explain: Collecting only in the morning narrows what is seen, which weakens validity, limits the time spent in the field and cuts off informants who are available only later in the day. All three are affected.

questions.stem: When Bryan accuses Paul of speaking “hoity toity” in line 3, Bryan is suggesting that Paul is using language to
questions.explain: “Hoity toity” and “speaky spokey” mock speech that sounds posh, so Bryan feels Paul is trying to show sophistication. Assert authority (A) is tempting, but Bryan objects to Paul sounding superior, not to Paul giving orders.

questions.stem:
Which of the following factors would affect dialectal varieties used by the various speakers in the scenario?
I. Audience
II. Occasion
III. Purpose
questions.explain: The speakers’ choice of variety depends on who they are talking to (audience), the situation (occasion) and what they want to achieve (purpose). Samantha says she would use Standard English for an interview, which shows occasion and purpose at work.

questions.stem: Which of the speakers advocate using language as identification?
questions.explain: Samantha and Bryan both defend their Creole as part of who they are, using language as identification. Any option with Paul is wrong, because he argues for Standard English and calls Creole “broken language”.

questions.stem: When a speaker changes his language use between Caribbean Standard English and Creole English during a conversation he is said to be
questions.explain: Moving between two language varieties within one conversation is called code switching. Dialect switching (C) and language switching (D) sound similar, but they are not the accepted linguistic terms.

questions.stem: Which of the following reveals that Simone thinks she is speaking ‘proper English’?
options: She does not condone village gossip.
She does not listen to the village gossip.
She uses the phrase “why allyuh cyah talk proper … like me?”
Martha asks her, “Buh wha is your problem, girl?”
questions.explain: Simone criticises others for not talking “proper … like me”, so her words show she believes she speaks proper English, even though “allyuh” and “cyah” are Creole forms. Option A is tempting, but gossip has nothing to do with language.

questions.stem: In which of the following quotations from the passage is an attitude to language reflected?
options: “I come to tell you some juicy stories”
“She neighbour was peeping through she fence last week.”
“Da’s how I does talk and ah proud fuh so.”
questions.explain: “Da’s how I does talk and ah proud fuh so” directly states Martha’s pride in her way of speaking, so it reflects an attitude to language. Option C is tempting because it is Creole, but it simply passes on gossip.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements BEST explains the meaning of the term ‘lingua franca’?
options: A language which is derived from French and used by African slaves
Any language which is native to African peoples who have been transplanted
A common language used in dialogue by persons with different native languages
Any language which is foreign to a speaker who moves to a new speech community
questions.explain: A lingua franca is a shared language that lets people with different first languages communicate. Option A is a trap built on the word “franca”; the term has nothing to do with French specifically.

questions.stem: An English Creole may be defined as a language
options: used by the poorest people in the society
only understood by some persons in the society
developed from contact between European and African languages
questions.explain: English Creoles developed from contact between European (English) and African languages during colonisation and slavery. Options A, B and C repeat common prejudices; Creoles are full languages used across society.

questions.stem: In which of the following expressions is the process of reduplication evident?
questions.explain: “Chaka-chaka” repeats a word to create a new meaning (untidy or messy), which is reduplication. “Eye-water” (B) is tempting because of the hyphen, but it is a calque, a compound translated from an African language pattern.

questions.stem: What does Percy’s statement “He should know that people don’t talk so in church” suggest?
options: Mavis’ grandson is disrespectful in church.
Percy does not like Mavis’ grandson.
Context is critical to the choice of code.
questions.explain: Percy’s objection is that this way of speaking does not suit a church service, so his point is that the setting should shape the code chosen. Option A is tempting, but Percy criticises the language used, not the grandson’s behaviour.

questions.stem: From Percy’s statements, what are the two varieties of language MOST likely spoken by Mavis’ grandchildren?
questions.explain: One grandchild spoke “so nice, like the people in the television shows”, suggesting Standard English, and the other said “I and I”, a marker of Rastafarian English. Option C is tempting, but “Television English” is not a recognised variety.

questions.stem: Which of the following contexts of communication BEST describes the interaction between the two groups of students?
questions.explain: The students come from two different countries and cultures, Jamaica and Cuba, so their interaction is intercultural. Interpersonal (C) is tempting, but it does not capture the cultural difference that defines this exchange.

questions.stem: While in Cuba the students attended a seminar. The guest speaker noticed that many of the visitors seemed restless during his presentation, even though he was speaking audibly. Which of the following was NOT likely responsible for their restlessness?
options: He was speaking in a monotone.
He was using many unfamiliar words.
He complemented his speech with projected slides.
questions.explain: Slides that complement a speech usually help an audience stay focused. Speaking too fast, in a monotone or with unfamiliar words (A–C) would all make listeners restless, so D is NOT a likely cause.

questions.stem: At which stage of the communication process does Sally generate ideas for her speech?
questions.explain: Generating ideas happens at the conceptualizing stage, before the message is encoded and sent. Decoding and interpreting (A, B) are done by the receiver, and feedback (D) comes after the message has been received.

questions.stem: Which of the following BEST explains why some students were “covering their mouths and snickering”?
options: They were angry at Sally’s choice of words.
They were amused by Sally’s choice of words.
questions.explain: Hiding their mouths while snickering shows that the students found Sally’s wording funny, for example “We all black.” Anger (C) is tempting, but snickering signals amusement rather than anger.

questions.stem: Barry’s use of “cool” in Frame 5 is an example of
questions.explain: “Cool”, meaning good or fashionable, is informal vocabulary popular with young people, which is slang. Jargon (B) is the specialist language of a profession, and dialect (C) is a whole regional variety, not one trendy word.

questions.stem: A student’s expository essay should typically aim to
questions.explain: Expository writing explains and informs, so it aims to enlighten and instruct the reader. Presenting a personal viewpoint (D) belongs to argument, and recounting experiences (B) belongs to narrative.

questions.stem: Which of the following would be the MAIN organizational strategy used in an expository essay on the topic “Types of Luxury Vehicles”?
questions.explain: An essay on “types” of vehicles sorts them into groups, which is classification. Comparison and contrast (D) is tempting, but the topic asks you to identify categories, not to weigh two things against each other.

questions.stem: Which of the following elements is typically NOT used in exposition?
questions.explain: Exposition relies on facts, statistics, expert information and supporting details to explain objectively. Emotive language aims to stir feelings, which suits persuasion, so it is typically NOT used in exposition.

questions.stem: Which of the following could be an advantage if Haldane conducted interviews?
options: High reliability of the information to be collected
In-depth nature of the information to be collected
questions.explain: Interviews let the researcher ask follow-up questions and gather detailed, in-depth answers. Cost effectiveness and wide coverage (A, B) are strengths of questionnaires, since interviews take time and usually cover a small area.

questions.stem: Haldane found an article entitled “Modern Technology Causing Canadian Students to Fail”. This article could be useful to his research as it
questions.explain: An article written by someone else is secondary data that can give Haldane background for his study. Option A is tempting, but an article is not automatically reliable, and this one is about Canadian students, not his school.

questions.stem: Which of the following factors could invalidate the generalization which Ms Davis makes from the findings?
options: The sample size is too large.
The sample is not representative of the population.
The research is carried out only in Ms Davis’ school.
The research is conducted during end of year examination.
questions.explain: A generalisation is only valid if the sample represents the population, so an unrepresentative sample undermines it. Option C is tempting, but researching one school is fine when her conclusions are only about that school.

questions.stem: The writer’s use of English Creole throughout the extract suggests that English Creole
options: is used only by illiterate people
should not be used for literary purposes
questions.explain: By telling the story in Creole, the writer treats it as a genuine language able to carry serious literature. Options A, C and D express negative attitudes that the extract itself contradicts.

questions.stem: Which of the following does NOT convey a communicative behaviour?
options: “From then on things got from bad to worse.”
“The wife and stepfather look like they real vex with Ascot.”
questions.explain: “From then on things got from bad to worse” is the narrator’s summary of events, not an action that sends a message. Snapping, sitting apart and looking vexed (A, B, D) all communicate feelings through behaviour.

questions.stem: Which of the following roles is language serving in this extract when it is used to judge Rufus’ level of education?
questions.explain: Judging someone’s education by the way he speaks is a social role of language: speech is used to rank people and decide who is fit to lead. Political (C) is tempting because of the Council, but the judgement itself is social.

questions.stem: The narrator relates the stories about Rufus MAINLY to
options: show that the people dislike Rufus
validate the view that Rufus is competent
questions.explain: Each story shows Rufus stumbling over words (“BRED”, “boys” for “buoys”), so the narrator tells them mainly to show that Rufus is uneducated. Option C is tempting, but “Rufus was all right”; people simply would not vote for him.

questions.stem: Which of the following terms refers to the range of language choices available to a speaker for use in different situations?
questions.explain: Register refers to the range of language choices a speaker makes to suit different situations, from formal to casual. Dialect (A) is tempting, but a dialect is a variety linked to a region or social group, not to the situation.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of the use of language performing a social function?
questions.explain: Introducing oneself builds and maintains relationships with other people, which is a social function of language. Praying silently and writing a journal entry (A, D) are personal, and reading a comic strip (C) is mainly for entertainment.

questions.stem: You anticipate that some of the students might easily forget Kristen’s manifesto. Which of the following actions would make the manifesto more memorable?
questions.explain: Slogans and jingles are short, catchy and repeated, which makes them easy to remember. Charts and graphs (A) are tempting, but they suit detailed information, not a campaign message students must recall.

questions.stem: Which of the following non-verbal communication methods would be MOST effective in helping Kristen enhance her presentation to the audience?
questions.explain: Gestures support and emphasise what Kristen says as she speaks, making her presentation livelier. Dress (A) is tempting, but it creates a first impression rather than enhancing the delivery itself.

questions.stem: Which of the following audience reactions would indicate that the upper school students are likely to vote for Kristen?
options: Looking at her while she speaks
Discussing her main points with friends
Applauding whenever she makes a point
questions.explain: Applauding each point is positive feedback that shows agreement, so it suggests the students are likely to vote for her. Looking at her (A) shows only attention, and loud rumbling (B) suggests restlessness or disapproval.

questions.stem: The purpose of the shell on the beach in the advertisement is to
options: share the diverse fauna of the islands
suggest the islands as a tropical escape
serve as a universal symbol of tourism
ensure that the composition is balanced
questions.explain: A shell on a quiet beach calls up sun, sand and sea, presenting the islands as a tropical escape. Option A is tempting, but a single shell is not meant to show the range of wildlife on the islands.

questions.stem: One possible reason for including the tag line, ‘The beach is only the beginning’ is to
options: indicate that this destination is unique
celebrate geographical diversity inclusive of coastal areas
indicate national pride in the country inclusive of beaches
suggest the island’s varied attractions beyond the beaches
questions.explain: Saying the beach is only “the beginning” promises much more to enjoy beyond the shore. Option A is tempting, but the tag line is about the variety of attractions, not about the destination being unique.

questions.stem: A student’s expository essay should typically aim to
questions.explain: Expository writing explains and informs, so it aims to enlighten and instruct the reader. Presenting a personal viewpoint (D) belongs to argument, and recounting experiences (B) belongs to narrative.

questions.stem: Which of the following would be the MAIN organizational strategy used in an expository essay on the topic: “Types of luxury vehicles”?
questions.explain: An essay on “types” of luxury vehicles sorts them into groups, which is classification. Comparison and contrast (D) is tempting, but the topic asks for categories, not a weighing up of two things.

questions.stem: Which of the following organizational features of language is typically NOT used in exposition?
questions.explain: Exposition relies on facts, statistics, expert information and supporting details to explain objectively. Emotive language aims to stir feelings, which suits persuasion, so it is typically NOT used in exposition.

questions.stem: Which of the following would be the MOST appropriate way to share the information with your audience?
questions.explain: Kindergarten children respond best to lively pictures and simple spoken explanations, so animation with speech suits them. A PowerPoint presentation (D) is tempting, but text-based slides would not hold young children’s attention.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the sequence that the presenter should follow to successfully complete the communication process?
options: Encoding the message, selecting the channel, selecting audience, disseminating the message
Encoding the message, transmitting the message, selecting channel, disseminating the message
Conceiving the message, encoding the message, selecting the channel, disseminating the message
Conceiving the message, interpreting the feedback, selecting audience, disseminating the message
questions.explain: A message must first be conceived, then encoded into words or images, then sent through a chosen channel to the audience. The other options start with encoding or put feedback before the message has even been sent.

questions.stem: Which of the following would be the MAIN advantage, to the researcher, if precoded questions were used as the method of data collection?
options: Ability to probe for further details
questions.explain: Precoded questions offer fixed answer choices, so responses can be counted and analysed easily. Probing for further details (D) is a strength of open questions and interviews, not of precoded questions.

questions.stem: Which of the following does NOT reflect how an interview might be administered for this research?
options: Sending an email to a manager
Talking with a contact over the phone
questions.explain: An interview means questioning a person, whether by email, by phone or face to face. Taking note of certified vehicles is observation or document study, not an interview, so it does NOT reflect how an interview is administered.

questions.stem: Which of the following sources could provide the MOST useful information to help the researchers to identify the sample?
questions.explain: Class registers record attendance every day, so they show exactly which senior students attend irregularly. Form teachers (A) are tempting, but their knowledge is less complete and less precise than the written record.

questions.stem: Which of the following must the research company consider when selecting a sample?
options: How well the population is represented
questions.explain: A sample must represent the population so that the findings can be applied to the whole group. Option D is tempting, but respondents are chosen for representativeness, not for how knowledgeable they are.

questions.stem: If the research company used observation as a method of collecting data, which of the following could be an advantage?
options: Predicting the behaviour to be observed
Directly witnessing the behaviour of participants
Spending an extended period of time collecting data
Participants changing their behaviour while being observed
questions.explain: The main advantage of observation is that the researcher sees the behaviour directly instead of relying on what people say. Option D is actually a weakness of observation, because people may act differently when watched.

questions.stem: When Bryan accuses Paul of speaking “hoity toity” in line 3, Bryan is suggesting that Paul is using language to
questions.explain: “Hoity toity” and “speaky spokey” mock speech that sounds posh, so Bryan feels Paul is trying to show sophistication. Assert authority (A) is tempting, but Bryan objects to Paul sounding superior, not to Paul giving orders.

questions.stem: Which of the following factors would affect the dialectal varieties used by the various speakers?
questions.explain: Social class strongly shapes which variety people use and how they view Standard English and Creole, as Paul’s comments show. Intellectual capacity (D) is wrong; Samantha points out that they are all educated, whichever variety they use.

questions.stem: Which of the speakers advocate using language as a form of identification?
questions.explain: Samantha and Bryan both defend their Creole as part of who they are, using language as a form of identification. Any option with Paul is wrong, because he argues for Standard English and calls Creole “broken language”.

questions.stem: If a speaker changes his language use between Caribbean Standard English and Creole English during a conversation, he would be engaging in
questions.explain: Moving between two language varieties during a conversation is code switching. Code mixing (A) is tempting, but it describes blending elements of both codes within a single sentence rather than switching between them.

questions.stem: Which of the following quotes from the dialogue is NOT an example of Creole syntax?
options: “sittin in front ah dat chupid computer” (lines 1–2)
“So you’s comin to de market wit me in de morning.” (line 4)
“Motherrr, … do I really have to do this?” (line 5)
questions.explain: Robbie’s “do I really have to do this?” follows Standard English grammar, so it is NOT Creole syntax. Option B is tempting because it looks the most English, but “in dat highfalutin language” still uses the Creole form “dat”.

questions.stem: Which of the following words describes the mother’s attitude towards her son’s “highfalutin language” (line 2)?
questions.explain: The mother calls the computer “chupid” and mocks his “highfalutin language”, which shows scorn. Proud (B) is tempting, but she is irritated by the way he now speaks, not proud of it.

questions.stem: Which of the following expressions BEST explains the meaning of the term ‘lingua franca’?
options: A language which is derived from French and used by African slaves
Any language which is native to African peoples who have been transplanted
A common language used in dialogue by persons with different native languages
Any language which is foreign to a speaker who moves to a new speech community
questions.explain: A lingua franca is a shared language that lets people with different first languages communicate. Option A is a trap built on the word “franca”; the term has nothing to do with French specifically.

questions.stem: A Caribbean English Creole may be defined as a language
options: used by the poorest people in the society
understood only by some persons in the society
developed from contact between European and African languages
questions.explain: Caribbean English Creoles developed from contact between European and African languages during colonisation and slavery. Options A, B and C repeat common prejudices; Creoles are full languages used across society.

questions.stem: Which of the following contexts of communication BEST describes the interaction between the two groups of students?
questions.explain: The students come from two different countries and cultures, Jamaica and Cuba, so their interaction is intercultural. Interpersonal (C) is tempting, but it does not capture the cultural difference that defines this exchange.

questions.stem: While in Cuba the students attended a seminar. The guest speaker noticed that many of the visitors seemed restless during his presentation, even though he was speaking audibly. Which of the following was LEAST likely to be responsible for their restlessness?
options: He was speaking in a monotone.
He was using many unfamiliar words.
He complemented his speech with projected slides.
questions.explain: Slides that complement a speech usually help an audience stay focused. Speaking too fast, in a monotone or with unfamiliar words (A–C) would all make listeners restless, so D is the LEAST likely cause.

questions.stem: In which of the following forms of communication is the communicator both the source and the destination of the message?
questions.explain: In intrapersonal communication you communicate with yourself, as in thinking or self-talk, so you are both source and destination. Interpersonal (C) is tempting, but it always involves at least two people.

questions.stem: Benjamin is concerned about his friend’s
questions.explain: Talking directly in his face and touching his hands concern personal space and closeness, which is proxemics. Vocalics (A) is tempting, but it refers to qualities of the voice, which are not his concern.

questions.stem: Which of the following techniques could Sandra use to boost her confidence when delivering the speech?
options: Pacing the room and avoiding eye contact
Reading directly from her prepared speech
Looking periodically at the teacher who is grading her
questions.explain: Making eye contact with friendly listeners and drawing on their nods and smiles can build a nervous speaker’s confidence. Reading from her script (C) is tempting, but it would weaken her connection with the audience.

questions.stem: The students’ expository essays should typically aim to
questions.explain: Expository writing explains and informs, so it aims to enlighten and instruct the reader. Presenting a viewpoint (C) belongs to argument, and recounting experiences (B) belongs to narrative.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT an organizational strategy that the students should typically use in their expository essays?
questions.explain: Classification, chronological order and comparison and contrast are standard ways of organising exposition. Narration tells a story, which belongs to narrative writing, so it is NOT a typical expository strategy.

questions.stem: The expression “Bread and water for a week” is effective in communicating the fact that
options: there was scarcity in the institution
questions.explain: The phrase names the punishment the narrator expects if she is caught, which shows that Matron enforces the rules strictly. It is about discipline, not about the girls’ normal meals or a shortage of food.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT an emotion experienced by the narrator in the passage?
questions.explain: The narrator is afraid, full of trepidation and anxious about what will happen if anyone speaks to her. She is anything but indifferent: she cares a great deal about being caught.

questions.stem: Which of the following would be the MAIN advantage if interviews are used as the method of data collection?
options: Ability to probe for further details
Ease in processing the data gathered
questions.explain: In an interview the researcher can ask follow-up questions and probe for more detail. Interviews are costly and time-consuming, are not anonymous, and give data that is harder to process than questionnaire answers.

questions.stem: Which of the following web addresses is NOT likely to provide the most credible information for this research?
questions.explain: A “.com” site is usually commercial and may aim to sell rather than inform. Government (.gov), educational (.edu) and non-profit (.org) sites are generally treated as more credible.

questions.stem: The MOST reliable source of primary data for this research would be
questions.explain: Primary data comes first-hand from the people being studied. Secondary school students include the 14–16 age group and can report their own reading habits; periodicals and newspapers are secondary sources.

questions.stem: Which of the following activities would Meghan and Lucy be involved in if they are conducting a survey?
options: Creating and investigating a treatment group
Gathering the sample’s opinions and beliefs
Obtaining detailed information on a member of the sample
questions.explain: A survey collects the opinions, beliefs and habits of a sample. A treatment group belongs to an experiment, diagnosing and solving problems is action research, and studying one member in depth is a case study.

questions.stem: Which of the following factors could invalidate the generalization which Ms Davis may make from the findings?
options: The sample size is too large.
The sample is not representative of the population.
The research is carried out only in Ms Davis’ school.
The research is conducted during end of year examinations.
questions.explain: Findings can only be generalized if the sample represents the population. A large sample does not weaken a study, and because her population is her own school, carrying out the research there is appropriate.

questions.stem: Which of the following types of registers is used in the dialogue?
questions.explain: The old man talks to his wife and neighbour in a relaxed, informal way, full of exclamations and dialect. That is casual register; nothing about the exchange is fixed, ceremonial or academic.

questions.stem: The speaker’s MAIN purpose for writing this letter is to
options: protest against police brutality and injustice
apologize for being locked up along with Jim
inform his mother of his current address and to console her
tell his mother that he and Jim are in jail and to explain why
questions.explain: Sonny writes to break the news that Jim was arrested and that he is now in prison, and to explain how it happened. The poet may be protesting injustice, but within the letter Sonny’s purpose is to inform and explain.

questions.stem: Based on the tone of the letter, the relationship between receiver and sender may be described as
questions.explain: “Dear Mama”, his hope that she is in good health and his sorrow at failing to protect Jim show warmth and love. “Cordial” only means polite and friendly, which is too distant for this son and mother.

questions.stem: Sonny is MOST likely to be incarcerated in
questions.explain: The address, “Jebb Avenue, S.W. 2 Inglan”, is a London prison address, and “Inglan” is the Creole spelling of England. His Jamaican Creole shows where Sonny comes from, not where he is held.

questions.stem: The narrator relates the stories about Rufus MAINLY to
options: show that the people dislike Rufus
validate the view that Rufus is incompetent
questions.explain: The “B-R-E-D-A” and “buoys/boys” stories illustrate the point that “Rufus don’t have the education”. The narrator says “Rufus was all right”, so he neither hates him nor thinks him useless.

questions.stem: Which of the following relationships between education and language is MOST evident in the scenario?
options: Only educated people use correct language.
Language use is indicative of one’s education level.
Education negatively impacts one’s use of language.
Education causes one to forget one’s mother tongue.
questions.explain: Iberry links Marcel’s Standard English to his studies abroad, so the way a person speaks is taken as a sign of education. Iberry went to high school and still uses Creole, so education has not erased his mother tongue.

questions.stem: Which of the following grammatical features is evident in the expression “Me ain’t have no money”?
questions.explain: “Ain’t” and “no” are two negatives in the same clause, a common Creole feature (double or multiple negation). Nothing is moved to the front of the sentence for emphasis.

questions.stem: What context of communication is depicted in the conversation?
questions.explain: The conversation is between two people, so it is interpersonal communication. A small group needs at least three people, and intrapersonal communication takes place within one person.

questions.stem: Which of the following audience reactions would indicate that the upper school students are likely to vote for Kristen?
options: Looking at her while she speaks
Discussing her main points with friends
Applauding whenever she makes a point
questions.explain: Applause after each point is clear positive feedback that shows agreement. Looking at her shows only attention, and talking about her points with friends could signal doubt just as easily as support.

questions.stem:
Which of the following are barriers to communication in the scenario?
I. Poor visual aids
II. Listeners’ attitude
III. Broken air conditioner
questions.explain: Unhelpful visual aids, Simon’s negative attitude and the discomfort caused by the broken air conditioning all interfere with the message, so all three are barriers.

questions.stem: The process by which messages are exchanged and meanings interpreted between the speaker and the audience is known as
questions.explain: Communication is the whole two-way process of sending messages and interpreting their meaning. Encoding and decoding are single stages within that process.

questions.stem: A student’s expository essay typically aims to
questions.explain: Expository writing explains and informs. Stirring emotions and presenting a viewpoint are aims of persuasive writing, and recounting experiences is narrative writing.

questions.stem: One organizational feature of language that is NOT typically found in expository text is the use of
questions.explain: Expository writing aims to be objective, so it relies on facts, expert information and supporting details. Emotive language belongs to persuasive writing.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the correct sequence that a presenter should follow to successfully complete the communication process?
options: Encoding the message, selecting the channel, selecting the audience, disseminating the message
Conceiving the message, encoding the message, selecting the channel, disseminating the message
Encoding the message, transmitting the message, selecting the channel, disseminating the message
Conceiving the message, interpreting the feedback, selecting the audience, disseminating the message
questions.explain: A sender first conceives the idea, then encodes it in words or symbols, chooses a suitable channel and finally sends it out. You cannot encode before having an idea, and feedback comes only after the message is received.

questions.stem: Which of the following strategies could help Sandra make a successful delivery?
options: Pacing the room and avoiding eye contact
Reading directly from her prepared speech
Keeping her eyes fixed on the overhead projector
questions.explain: Finding a friendly, encouraging face in the audience helps a nervous speaker stay calm and keep eye contact. Pacing, reading straight from the script or staring at the projector all weaken delivery.

questions.stem: The use of the expression ‘unwavering smell of baking and cooking’ suggests that the smell was
questions.explain: “Unwavering” means steady and never changing, so the smell was constant. “Intermittent” means the opposite, and the word itself says nothing about whether the smell was pleasant or strong.

questions.stem: Which of the following would be the MAIN advantage, to the researchers, if precoded questions were used as the method of data collection?
options: Ability to probe for further details
questions.explain: Precoded (closed) questions offer fixed answer choices that are already coded, so the responses can be counted and analysed quickly. They do not allow probing, which is a strength of interviews.

questions.stem: Which of the following does NOT reflect how an interview might be administered for this research?
options: Sending an email to a manager
Talking with a contact over the phone
questions.explain: Noting which vehicles are certified is observation or a document check: no one is being asked questions. Interviews can be held face to face, by telephone or even by email.

questions.stem: A reliable source of secondary data for the research would be
questions.explain: Newspaper articles report information already gathered by others, so they are secondary sources; the research itself began with a news report. Licensing officers and buyers would give first-hand (primary) data.

questions.stem: Which of the following strategies is MOST likely to help the reader of the written report to easily access specific information?
options: Numbering the pages and indenting content
Using bold font throughout the document
Having headings and subheadings of main topics
Displaying information using charts and graphs
questions.explain: Headings and subheadings act as signposts, so readers can go straight to the section they need. Bold text everywhere removes emphasis, and charts present data but do not help readers find it.

questions.stem: Which of the following would be an ADVANTAGE to the research company if it used observation as a data collection method?
options: Predicting the behaviour to be observed
Directly witnessing the behaviour of participants
Spending an extended period of time collecting data
Participants changing their behaviour while being observed
questions.explain: Observation lets researchers see what people actually do instead of relying on what they say. A long collection period and participants changing their behaviour when watched are disadvantages.

questions.stem: For which of the following reasons would a travel agent use Standard English and NOT Creole?
options: Standard English is superior to Creole.
Creole cannot be considered a language.
Creole is the majority language of the country.
Standard English is the official language of the country.
questions.explain: In a formal business setting, staff are expected to use the official language. Claiming that Standard English is “superior” or that Creole is not a language reflects prejudice, not linguistic fact.

questions.stem: Which of the following words describes Zan’s attitude to Kareem’s language?
questions.explain: Zan mocks Kareem for “talking yankee” before he has even left and asks, “Like we language ent good?”, which shows disapproval of the change in his speech.

questions.stem: Which of the following linguistic features is present in the terms “dat” and “dey”?
questions.explain: In “dat” and “dey” (that, there) the “th” sound is pronounced /d/. This is a difference in sound, so it is a phonological feature; the meaning and grammar stay the same.

questions.stem:
Which of the following circumstances determine the variety of English a speaker uses in a specific context?
I. The person with whom he/she speaks
II. The medium of communication
III. The attitude of the writer or speaker
questions.explain: Speakers adjust their language to the listener, to whether they are speaking or writing (the medium) and to their own attitude towards the situation. All three influence the variety chosen.

questions.stem: Face-to-face discourse in which participants alternate between producing spoken discourse and interpreting discourse produced by others is referred to as
questions.explain: Turn taking is the pattern of speaking and listening in turns during a conversation. A monologue has only one speaker, and an interruption breaks the turn-taking pattern.

questions.stem: Which of the following sentences MOST accurately outlines the central message of the advertisement?
options: Persons who hold meetings just want to avoid work and socialize.
Meetings merely allow for socializing, bragging and the wasting of company time.
Meetings are good places for showing off talents and skills.
Although meetings waste time, persons hold them because they are more practical.
questions.explain: The advert lists what meetings let you do (see people, feel important, eat donuts, impress colleagues) “All on company time!”, and calls them “the practical alternative to work”. The message is that meetings are socializing that wastes company time.

questions.stem: Which of the following fallacies is evident in the statement “All meetings are a waste of time”?
questions.explain: The word “All” turns some unproductive meetings into a claim about every meeting, without enough evidence. That is a hasty generalization. It does not claim that everyone believes it (bandwagon) or that one event caused another.

questions.stem: In which of the following contexts of communication is the communicator BOTH the source and the destination of the message?
questions.explain: In intrapersonal communication a person communicates with himself or herself, for example in thinking or self-talk, so the same person sends and receives the message.

questions.stem: Which of the following could MOST likely be considered a barrier in this communication context?
questions.explain: Students waiting in a lunch line are surrounded by chatter and movement, so external noise would make the message hard to hear. Good posture and eye contact help communication.

questions.stem: Which of the following techniques could Sandra use to boost her confidence when delivering the speech?
options: Pacing the room and avoiding eye contact
Reading directly from her prepared speech
Looking periodically at the teacher who is grading her
questions.explain: Connecting with friendly, attentive listeners and drawing on their positive reactions calms a nervous speaker. Avoiding eye contact, reading the script or watching the examiner tends to increase anxiety.

questions.stem: Sally’s aunt advised her to pronounce her words clearly as even a small miscommunication can have far reaching consequences for her message. To which of the following elements of speaking is her aunt referring?
questions.explain: Enunciation means pronouncing words clearly and distinctly. Projection is about volume, modulation is varying the voice, and stress is emphasis on particular syllables or words.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a feature of informal colloquial discourse?
options: Style is elevated with a variety of sentences.
Dialogue involves run-on sentences and ellipses.
Organization is systematic and well-thought out.
questions.explain: Everyday conversation is unplanned, so speakers run sentences together and leave words out (ellipsis). Unity, an elevated style and systematic organization are features of formal discourse.

questions.stem: The students’ expository essays should typically aim to
questions.explain: Expository writing explains a topic so that readers understand it better. Affecting emotions and presenting a viewpoint are persuasive aims, and recounting experiences is narrative.

questions.stem: Which of the following organizational patterns would the students use in a presentation about the different types of flora and fauna found in a nature reserve?
questions.explain: Presenting “different types” of plants and animals means sorting them into groups, which is classification. Temporal sequencing follows time order, and cause and effect explains why things happen.

questions.stem: Which of the following would be the MAIN advantage if interviews are used as the method of data collection?
options: Ease in processing the data gathered
Ability to probe for further details
Collection of primary and secondary data
questions.explain: Interviews let the researcher ask follow-up questions and probe for more detail. They are not anonymous, their data is harder to process than questionnaire data, and they collect primary data only.

questions.stem: Which of the following web addresses is NOT likely to provide the MOST credible information for this research?
questions.explain: A “.com” site is usually commercial and may aim to sell rather than inform. Government (.gov), educational (.edu) and non-profit (.org) sites are generally treated as more credible.

questions.stem: Which of the following would be the MAIN activity that Meghan and Lucy engage in if they are conducting a survey?
options: Creating and investigating a treatment group
Gathering the sample’s opinions and beliefs
Obtaining detailed information on a member of the sample
questions.explain: A survey collects the opinions, beliefs and habits of a sample. A treatment group belongs to an experiment, diagnosing and solving problems is action research, and studying one member in depth is a case study.

questions.stem: Which of the following facts about Komlin is suggested by both passages?
options: Komlin wanted to enjoy expensive things.
Komlin made use of the opportunity he was given.
He was once imprisoned but was later rescued.
He moved from poverty to having a crippling disease.
questions.explain: Extract 1 shows Komlin leaving poverty for “education and advancement”, and Extract 2 shows him as a chief accountant. Together they show he used his opportunity. The “crippling disease” is poverty itself, used as a metaphor.

questions.stem: Which of the following literary elements is used in BOTH extracts?
questions.explain: Both extracts explore the theme of escaping poverty through education and opportunity. Only Extract 1 evokes a setting (the dark, damp room), and the two are told from different angles.

questions.stem:
Which of the following quotations represent opinions?
I. “in this tiny, dark, damp room”
II. “is a member of three voluntary children’s assistance organizations”
III. “believes in helping children escape poverty”
questions.explain: Calling the room tiny, dark and damp is a personal judgement, and what Komlin believes is his opinion. His membership of three organizations can be checked, so it is a fact.

questions.stem: Which of the following literary devices accurately identifies the expression “wave of expectancy”?
questions.explain: Komlin’s growing excitement is described as a wave he floats on, a direct comparison without “like” or “as”, which is a metaphor. There is no contradiction, so it is not a paradox or an oxymoron.

questions.stem: When Bryan accuses Paul of speaking “hoity toity” in line 3, Bryan is suggesting that Paul is using language to
questions.explain: “Hoity toity” and “speaky spokey” describe speech that sounds posh or put on. Bryan feels Paul uses Standard English to appear refined and superior, that is, to show sophistication.

questions.stem:
Which of the following factors would affect the dialectal varieties used by the various speakers in the scenario?
I. Purpose
II. Occasion
III. Audience
questions.explain: Samantha says she would use Standard English for an interview but not with her friends, which shows that purpose, occasion and audience all shape the variety a speaker chooses.

questions.stem: Which of the following speakers advocate using language as identification?
questions.explain: Samantha uses Creole with her friends, and Bryan proudly names his speech “Caribbean Creole English”, so both tie language to who they are. Paul wants everyone to use Standard English and calls Creole “broken”.

questions.stem: The register used by the speaker in the poem may be described as
questions.explain: This is a son writing to his mother in their home language, beginning “Dear Mama”. Communication between close family members is intimate register.

questions.stem: Sonny is MOST likely to be incarcerated in
questions.explain: The address, “Jebb Avenue, S.W. 2 Inglan”, is a London prison address, and “Inglan” is the Creole spelling of England. His Jamaican Creole shows where Sonny comes from, not where he is held.

questions.stem: Based on the tone of the letter, the relationship between receiver and sender may be described as
questions.explain: “Dear Mama”, his hope that she is in good health and his sorrow at failing to protect Jim show warmth and love. “Cordial” only means polite and friendly, which is too distant for this son and mother.

questions.stem: Which of the following features of language do Creole and Standard English have in common?
questions.explain: Every language is human, rule-governed (systematic) and learned rather than instinctive. No language is static, and prestige is a social value given to Standard English, not a feature shared with Creole.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the MOST promoted reason for Caribbean speakers to be proficient in the use of standard languages?
options: Unlike the official varieties, the Creole is not language.
The Creole cannot carry messages in the same way standard varieties can.
The standard language is easier to understand.
Socioeconomic advancement is associated with the standard variety.
questions.explain: Standard English is used in education, business and government, so mastering it is linked to better jobs and social mobility. The other options are myths: Creole is a full language that can carry any message.

questions.stem: Which of the following technologies does NOT allow users to interface with Internet content?
questions.explain: A CD only stores data; it cannot connect to the Internet or display online content by itself. A tablet connects directly, and many cameras and projectors can share or display Internet content.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of formal technical discourse?
options: The tone is objective and serious.
The organization is clear, logical and coherent.
The language is simple and conversational.
There is a heavy content load, depth of thought and cogency.
questions.explain: Technical discourse is objective, logical and dense with content, and its language is precise and specialized. Simple, conversational language belongs to informal discourse.

questions.stem: An example of vertical communication within an organization is a meeting of
options: heads of department from different branches
managers and assistants from different branches
questions.explain: Vertical communication flows between different levels of an organization, such as managers and their assistants. The other options bring together people at the same level, which is horizontal communication.

questions.stem: The purpose of the shell on the beach in the advertisement is to
options: share the diverse fauna of the islands
suggest that the islands are a tropical escape
serve as a universal symbol of tourism
ensure that the composition is balanced
questions.explain: A conch shell resting on white sand instantly suggests a quiet tropical beach and invites viewers to imagine escaping there. The single shell is not there to show the islands’ wildlife or to balance the layout.

questions.stem: The process by which messages are exchanged and meanings interpreted between the speaker and the audience is known as
questions.explain: Communication is the whole two-way process of sending messages and interpreting their meaning. Encoding and decoding are single stages within that process.

questions.stem: The MAIN point which a speaker makes while delivering a speech is known as the
questions.explain: The thesis statement sets out the central point that the whole speech develops. Supporting details back it up, and a purpose statement says what the speaker hopes to achieve.

questions.stem: Which of the following introductory strategies would be MOST effective for a speaker whose audience is young and has a limited attention span?
questions.explain: A short, funny story grabs young listeners’ attention quickly and keeps them interested. A definition is dry, and a riddle or paradox may demand more concentration than this audience will give.

questions.stem: For which of the following organizational patterns does a speaker start by discussing the least important idea and discussing the most important last?
questions.explain: Ascending order builds from the least to the most important point, so the strongest idea comes last. Space order follows location, and sequential order follows steps or time.

questions.stem: The students’ expository essays should typically aim to
questions.explain: Expository writing explains a topic so that readers understand it better. Affecting emotions and presenting a viewpoint are persuasive aims, and recounting experiences is narrative.

questions.stem: Which of the following organizational patterns would the students use in a presentation about the different types of flora and fauna found in a nature reserve?
questions.explain: Presenting “different types” of plants and animals means sorting them into groups, which is classification. Temporal sequencing follows time order, and cause and effect explains why things happen.

questions.stem: Which of the following would be the MAIN advantage, to the researchers, if precoded questions are used as the method of data collection?
options: Ability to probe for further details
questions.explain: Precoded (closed) questions give answers in fixed categories, so results can be counted and analysed quickly. Probing for details (D) is an advantage of interviews, not of precoded questions.

questions.stem: Which of the following does NOT reflect how an interview might be administered for this research?
options: Sending an email to a manager
Talking with a contact over the phone
questions.explain: An interview needs an exchange with a respondent, whether by email, telephone or face to face. Noting certified vehicles is observation or record checking, so it is not a way of administering an interview.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT considered a scholarly website?
