questions.explain: Scholarly sites give access to peer-reviewed work by experts. Google Scholar, Oxford Academic and SAGE all do this, but anyone can edit Wikipedia, so it is not a scholarly source.

questions.stem: Ravi has been accused of bias by his friends. Which of the following BEST describes what his friends refer to?
options: He often disagrees with their views
He easily changes his mind on an issue
He holds to views regardless of the facts
He is inconsistent when it comes to religion
questions.explain: Bias means holding to a view out of personal preference even when the facts point elsewhere. Disagreeing with friends (A) or changing one’s mind (B) is not bias in itself.

questions.stem:
Which of the following is the BEST evidence of a fact?
I. Based on strong beliefs and judgment
II. Proven to be true based on objective proof
III. Can be verified through observation or experimentation
questions.explain: A fact can be proven with objective evidence and checked through observation or experiment (II and III). Statement I describes an opinion, which rests on beliefs and judgment.

questions.stem: Which of the following grammatical features is reflected in the expression “The man have a heart of a child”?
questions.explain: Standard English would need “has” to agree with “the man”. Creole leaves the verb unmarked, so “have” is used with a singular subject. Nothing is front-focused (B) and the sentence is not about past time (C).

questions.stem: Which of the following phonological features is reflected in the word “dat”?
options: ‘d’ replaces a voiced ‘th’ at the end of the word
‘d’ replaces a voiceless ‘th’ at the end of the word
‘d’ replaces a voiceless ‘th’ at the beginning of the word
‘d’ replaces a voiced ‘th’ at the beginning of the word
questions.explain: “That” begins with a voiced “th” sound, as in “this”, and Creole replaces it with “d”, giving “dat”. The change happens at the start of the word, so the options about the end of the word are wrong.

questions.stem: Which of the following grammatical features is reflected in the expression “When his pappa come from Cayenne and die Belle Maison, he take the cuatro”?
questions.explain: The events happened in the past, yet “come”, “die” and “take” carry no past-tense marking. This unmarked past tense is a common feature of Caribbean Creoles.

questions.stem: Sunil’s mother notices that since he started staying out late with a local gang of boys he has started to speak and sound like them. Her priest tells her such in-group use of language is a danger sign. The group’s use of language can BEST be described as
questions.explain: Argot is the secret, in-group language of a particular group, often one outside the mainstream, such as a gang. Dialect (C) and vernacular (D) are varieties used by whole communities.

questions.stem:
“Is me”, the boy answered.
“No William, that’s not English. It is I.”
“You sure Miss. Dat don’t sound right”
As a speaker of Creole English, what accounts for the challenge William has in distinguishing between Creole English and Standard English?
options: Standard English has many contradictory rules
Standard English rules depend on the country in which you live
Creole speakers often substitute object pronouns for subject ones
Creole speakers do not understand that it has no set rules or structure
questions.explain: William says “Is me”, using the object pronoun “me” where Standard English uses the subject pronoun “I”. Creole commonly does this, so the Standard form sounds wrong to him. D is false: Creole has its own rules.

questions.stem: Which of the following grammatical features is reflected in the expression “dem woman eh easy”?
questions.explain: “Dem woman” refers to more than one woman, yet “woman” has no plural ending; “dem” shows the plural instead. This is an unmarked plural noun.

questions.stem: Which audience is the flyer MOST likely targeting?
questions.explain: A community fair held at the community playfield is aimed at the people who live in that community. The other options describe audiences that are too broad or are not suggested by the flyer.

questions.stem: How could this message be made more appropriate for distribution via social media?
questions.explain: On social media, hyperlinks let readers click straight through to more details, directions or tickets. Text language only (C) would make the message less clear, and a template (D) does not adapt the message to the medium.

questions.stem:
Which of the following would MOST likely make the message more appealing to a younger audience?
I. Using high-quality graphics.
II. Including a reference to popular entertainers.
III. Stating that there will be prizes and surprises.
questions.explain: Young people respond to attractive graphics, familiar entertainers and the promise of prizes and surprises, so all three would make the message more appealing to them.

questions.stem: Sally’s aunt advised her to pronounce her words clearly as even a small miscommunication can have far-reaching consequences for her message. To which of the following elements of speaking is her aunt referring?
questions.explain: Enunciation is pronouncing words clearly and distinctly, which is exactly what the aunt advises. Projection (B) makes the voice carry, and modulation (C) varies pitch and tone.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a feature of informal colloquial discourse?
options: Style is elevated with a variety of sentences.
Dialogue involves run-on sentences and ellipses.
Organization is systematic and well thought out.
questions.explain: Informal, colloquial talk is spontaneous, so it often has run-on sentences and ellipses (words left out). The other options describe planned, formal discourse.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the BEST explanation of argumentation?
options: Appeal to feelings and emotions to change action or belief
Appeal to basic wants, desires and needs to change behaviour
Use of strategies to manipulate and take advantage of persons
Use of logic and reason to bring about change in action or belief
questions.explain: Argumentation uses logic, reasons and evidence to change what people believe or do. Appealing mainly to feelings (A) or needs (B) is persuasion, and manipulation (C) is not legitimate argument.

questions.stem:
Description of the original stimulus: A bar graph produced by Mrs Caro, head of marketing for Elantrics, a new sports store. It shows the level of interest in three types of sporting goods (gym wear, sporting goods and equipment) for three age groups: 15–19, 20–30 and 31–40 years. The values on the original graph are not reproduced here.

Mrs Caro made a claim that cost was a reason for the low level of interest in equipment.
Which of the following statements adequately describes this claim?
options: It is valid given what is known about the price of equipment.
The claim is reliable as it is supported by a number of respondents.
It is invalid as the sample size is too small to support that conclusion.
The claim is invalid as the expense variable is not mentioned in the data.
questions.explain: A valid claim must be supported by the data collected. The graph measures interest only and says nothing about price, so the claim about cost cannot be supported. A relies on outside assumptions, not on the research.

questions.stem:
Description of the original stimulus: Two short extracts about the same man, Komlin.

Extract 1: Komlin’s resentment at living “in this tiny, dark, damp room” with scant, mismatched furniture fades. He is now “floating on a wave of expectancy”, and the beep-beep of the horn outside is the sweet sound of freedom from his pauper-like days into the brave new world of education and advancement.

Extract 2: Komlin McMain, chief accountant at Mang and Associates, “is a member of three voluntary children’s assistance organizations”. He strongly “believes in helping children escape poverty”, the crippling disease from which he was rescued.

Which of the following literary devices accurately identifies the expression “wave of expectancy”?
questions.explain: Expectancy is not literally a wave; the writer compares Komlin’s rising excitement to a wave carrying him along, without using “like” or “as”. That makes it a metaphor.

questions.stem:
Description of the original stimulus: A short dialogue among three friends, Paul, Samantha and Bryan. Paul greets everyone in Standard English. Samantha replies in Creole that her foot is hurting. Bryan (line 3) complains that Paul keeps trying to “chat hoity toity, speaky spokey” and says he does not like it. Paul says they should speak Caribbean Standard English and not “some broken language”. Samantha says she is educated but does not have to use Standard English with her friends because she is not doing an interview. Bryan says he is not speaking a broken language but Caribbean Creole English.

When Bryan accuses Paul of speaking “hoity toity” (line 3), Bryan is suggesting that Paul is using language to
questions.explain: “Hoity toity” mocks someone who seems to be putting on airs. Bryan suggests that Paul uses Standard English to sound refined and superior, not to give orders (A) or comment on society (C).

questions.stem:
Description of the original stimulus: A short dialogue among three friends, Paul, Samantha and Bryan. Paul greets everyone in Standard English. Samantha replies in Creole that her foot is hurting. Bryan (line 3) complains that Paul keeps trying to “chat hoity toity, speaky spokey” and says he does not like it. Paul says they should speak Caribbean Standard English and not “some broken language”. Samantha says she is educated but does not have to use Standard English with her friends because she is not doing an interview. Bryan says he is not speaking a broken language but Caribbean Creole English.

Which of the following factors would affect the dialectal varieties used by the various speakers?
I. Purpose
II. Occasion
III. Audience
questions.explain: Speakers choose a variety according to why they are speaking, the occasion and who is listening. Samantha even says she would use Standard English for an interview but not with friends, so all three factors apply.

questions.stem:
Description of the original stimulus: A short dialogue among three friends, Paul, Samantha and Bryan. Paul greets everyone in Standard English. Samantha replies in Creole that her foot is hurting. Bryan (line 3) complains that Paul keeps trying to “chat hoity toity, speaky spokey” and says he does not like it. Paul says they should speak Caribbean Standard English and not “some broken language”. Samantha says she is educated but does not have to use Standard English with her friends because she is not doing an interview. Bryan says he is not speaking a broken language but Caribbean Creole English.

Which of the following speakers advocate using language as identification?
questions.explain: Samantha and Bryan defend using Creole with their friends as part of who they are, and Bryan names it Caribbean Creole English. Paul rejects Creole as “broken”, so the options that include him are wrong.

questions.stem:
Description of the original stimulus: A scene in a local market. A vendor calls out in Creole: “Come get yuh potato an yam!” Sandra asks the price in Standard English. The vendor answers, “De potato dem is six dollar a poun. How much yuh waa tuh buy?” Sandra: “I would like to buy five pounds, please. Yuh have change for a hundred-dollar bill?” Vendor: “Nah worry. Ah goin an geh change.”

The MOST likely reason for the vendor’s consistent use of Creole could be that she
questions.explain: The vendor understands Sandra’s Standard English and answers her, so she clearly knows it (A, C). She keeps to Creole because it is the code she is comfortable using in the market.

questions.stem:
Description of the original stimulus: A scene in a local market. A vendor calls out in Creole: “Come get yuh potato an yam!” Sandra asks the price in Standard English. The vendor answers, “De potato dem is six dollar a poun. How much yuh waa tuh buy?” Sandra: “I would like to buy five pounds, please. Yuh have change for a hundred-dollar bill?” Vendor: “Nah worry. Ah goin an geh change.”

Which of the following statements about the social setting in the scenario BEST explains the use of English Creole?
options: Uneducated people sell in the local market.
Uneducated people buy in the local market.
The local market is regarded as a vernacular setting.
The local market is seen as an intrapersonal setting.
questions.explain: A market is an informal, everyday setting where the vernacular is normal for buyers and sellers alike. A and B are prejudiced assumptions, and an intrapersonal setting (D) involves only oneself.

questions.stem:
Description of the original stimulus: A poem adapted from “Noh Lickle Twang” by Louise Bennett. The speaker scolds a Jamaican boy who has come home after six months in the United States showing no sign of having been there. She says: “Me glad fi see yuh come back, bwoy, / But lawd, yuh let me down. / Me shame a yuh so till alla / Me proudness drop a ground.” She asks how he could spend six whole months in ’Merica and come back “not a piece better”, with “Not even lickle language … Not even lickle twang”. In stanza 4 she says that his sister, after only one week with an American, “talk so nice now dat we have Dejooce fi understand”.

The Creole statement “Me proudness drop a ground” suggests that the speaker
options: is embarrassed by the actions of the boy
has fainted, causing him/her to be exposed
is frightened by the boy’s inconsideration
questions.explain: “Me proudness drop a ground” means the speaker’s pride has fallen to the ground. It is a figurative way of saying she is embarrassed by the boy, not that she literally fell (A) or fainted (C).

questions.stem:
Description of the original stimulus: A poem adapted from “Noh Lickle Twang” by Louise Bennett. The speaker scolds a Jamaican boy who has come home after six months in the United States showing no sign of having been there. She says: “Me glad fi see yuh come back, bwoy, / But lawd, yuh let me down. / Me shame a yuh so till alla / Me proudness drop a ground.” She asks how he could spend six whole months in ’Merica and come back “not a piece better”, with “Not even lickle language … Not even lickle twang”. In stanza 4 she says that his sister, after only one week with an American, “talk so nice now dat we have Dejooce fi understand”.

The poet does NOT use Jamaican Creole in the poem to
options: situate the poem in the Caribbean
show that Creole is a credible literary tool
demonstrate that the speaker is uneducated
questions.explain: Bennett uses Jamaican Creole to celebrate the vernacular, to set the poem in the Caribbean and to show that Creole is a credible literary tool. She is not trying to show that the speaker is uneducated.

questions.stem:
Description of the original stimulus: A poem adapted from “Noh Lickle Twang” by Louise Bennett. The speaker scolds a Jamaican boy who has come home after six months in the United States showing no sign of having been there. She says: “Me glad fi see yuh come back, bwoy, / But lawd, yuh let me down. / Me shame a yuh so till alla / Me proudness drop a ground.” She asks how he could spend six whole months in ’Merica and come back “not a piece better”, with “Not even lickle language … Not even lickle twang”. In stanza 4 she says that his sister, after only one week with an American, “talk so nice now dat we have Dejooce fi understand”.

What linguistic feature of the speaker’s language is represented in the use of the word “Dejooce” (stanza 4)?
questions.explain: “Dejooce” is spelt to capture how the speaker says the words, so it represents the sound system of her language, which is phonology. It has nothing to do with word order (A) or grammar (B).

questions.stem: If a speaker alternates between Caribbean Standard English and Creole English during a conversation, he would be engaging in
questions.explain: Alternating between Caribbean Standard English and Creole English within a conversation is code switching. Semantic substitution and differentiation (C, D) concern word meanings, not the choice of variety.

questions.stem: Language is capable of accommodating emerging concepts or ideas as society evolves. This means that one characteristic of language is that it is
questions.explain: A dynamic language changes and grows, adding words for new ideas and inventions. Systematic (B) means rule-governed, which is a different characteristic.

questions.stem:
Description of the original stimulus: An advertisement by Jason Fried, designed like a poster. It reads: “Are you lonely? Tired of working on your own? Do you hate making decisions? HOLD A MEETING! You can see people, show charts, feel important, point with a stick, eat donuts, impress your colleagues. All on company time! MEETINGS: THE PRACTICAL ALTERNATIVE TO WORK”.

Which of the following statements MOST accurately outlines the central message of the advertisement?
options: Meetings merely allow for socializing, bragging and the wasting of company time.
Although meetings waste time, persons hold them because they are more practical.
Meetings are good places for showing off talents and skills.
Persons who hold meetings try to avoid work on Fridays.
questions.explain: The advert lists socializing, showing off and eating donuts “on company time”, then calls meetings “the practical alternative to work”. Its sarcastic message is that meetings often waste time. B takes “practical” at face value.

questions.stem: After ending a three-hour meeting, an employee stated, “All meetings are a waste of time.” Which of the following fallacies is evident in the statement?
questions.explain: The employee judges all meetings on the basis of one long meeting. Drawing a sweeping conclusion from too little evidence is a hasty generalization. Bandwagon (A) would appeal to what everyone else thinks.

questions.stem: Which of the following contexts of communication can be used to describe a general election rally?
questions.explain: At an election rally a speaker addresses a large audience, which is public communication. Small-group communication (C) involves only a few people interacting closely.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a possible negative impact of the use of a word processor on students’ communication skills?
questions.explain: Students who type everything get fewer chances to practise writing by hand, so their handwriting may weaken. Typing has little to do with speaking (B), and more interaction or feedback (C, D) would not be negative.

questions.stem: Which of the following introductory strategies would be MOST effective for a speaker whose audience is young and has a limited attention span?
questions.explain: A short, funny story quickly grabs and holds the attention of a young audience. A definition (B) is dry, and a riddle or rhetorical question is over in a moment and may not hold attention as well.

questions.stem: In which of the following organizational patterns does a speaker start by discussing the least important idea first and the most important idea last?
questions.explain: Ascending (climactic) order builds from the least important point to the most important, saving the strongest point for last. Topical order (B) simply divides a subject into subtopics.

questions.stem: In online teaching, which of the following communication elements is MOST likely affected when students are muted?
questions.explain: When students are muted they cannot reply aloud, so the teacher loses their spoken feedback. Students can still decode the lesson; it is the return message that is cut off.

questions.stem: If David meets another speaker of English who has a challenge understanding his accent, which of the following features of vocal delivery should he adjust to facilitate clear communication?
questions.explain: Enunciation is pronouncing each word clearly and distinctly, which helps a listener who finds an accent hard to follow. Volume (A) and projection (B) make speech louder, not clearer.

questions.stem: The MAIN purpose of the monologue is to
options: verify that family members escaped the natural disaster
confirm that individuals could not sleep during the natural disaster
recall the confusion of an individual after the natural disaster
encourage family members to be careful when there is a natural disaster
questions.explain: The monologue relives one person’s bewilderment on waking after the eruption of La Soufrière, as questions like “What is going on here? What happen?” show. It does not give safety advice (D) or confirm that relatives escaped (A).

questions.stem: Which of the following devices are evident in the expression “whirring like supersonic jets”?
questions.explain: “Like supersonic jets” is a simile because it compares using “like”, and the comparison exaggerates the noise for effect, which is hyperbole. Without “like” it would be a metaphor (B, D).

questions.stem: The monologue MAINLY conveys the ideas relating to the event through
questions.explain: The monologue follows the event in time order, from falling asleep to waking and discovering what has happened. That is chronological sequencing, not classification or problem and solution.

questions.stem: The line “And not a soul not here” is effective in conveying that the persona
questions.explain: “Not a soul not here” uses a Creole double negative to stress that nobody else was there. The persona was alone, not dead (A) or vanished (C).

questions.stem: The rhetorical questions, “What is going on here? What happen?” are used in the monologue to
options: reveal that La Soufrière was present
convey that the persona was confused
questions.explain: The persona asks questions that no one is there to answer, which shows bewilderment. Rhetorical questions are not meant to get real answers, so B and A miss their purpose.

questions.stem: The colloquial expression “The dead couldn’t wake me” means the persona was
questions.explain: “The dead couldn’t wake me” is an exaggerated, everyday way of saying the persona slept so deeply that nothing could wake him. It has nothing to do with a graveyard (C).

questions.stem: Which of the following describe the tone used in the monologue?
questions.explain: The persona is worried and unsure about what has happened, so the tone is one of concern and uncertainty. There is no anger (A), excitement (C) or regret (D).

questions.stem: Which of the following media would be MOST effective for the students to inform residents about the research?
questions.explain: Rural residents, including older domino players, are most likely to read a newspaper and attend a town hall meeting. Blogs and websites (A, B, C) depend on internet access and may not reach them.

questions.stem: Which of the following are primary sources from which the students could gather information?
questions.explain: A primary source gives first-hand information. Interviews collect data directly from the players being studied; textbooks, internet searches and editorials are secondary sources.

questions.stem: Which of the following reflects the MOST effective way an interview may be administered for this research?
options: Conversing with residents face to face
questions.explain: Talking with residents face to face lets the students build trust, see reactions and ask follow-up questions. Facebook posts (C) are not interviews, and email (B) may not reach rural residents.

questions.stem: Which of the following would be the BEST data collection instrument for probing the issue being researched?
questions.explain: An interview schedule lets researchers probe sensitive issues such as anxiety and self-harm in depth and follow up on answers. Questionnaires (A) give limited, fixed responses that cannot be probed.

questions.stem: Which of the following may be the MOST reliable secondary source for providing data for the research?
questions.explain: A secondary source reports research done by others. Health magazines summarise findings on mental health for readers, whereas medical and school reports are first-hand records about individuals. Radio advertisements (D) are not reliable data.

questions.stem: If observation is used as a method of collecting data, which of the following could be an ADVANTAGE for the research team?
options: Predicting the behaviour to be observed
Spending an extended period collecting data
Witnessing natural behaviour directly as it occurs
questions.explain: Observation lets researchers see natural behaviour as it happens, instead of relying on what people say about themselves. They cannot predict (A) or control (B) the behaviour, and a long collection period (C) is a drawback.

questions.stem: Which of the following MUST the research teams consider when selecting a valid sample?
options: How regularly respondents use modern types of social media
The location of the educational institutions respondents attend
How well respondents are truly representative of the population
The knowledge respondents acquired from reading about mental health challenges
questions.explain: A valid sample must represent the population being studied, here young people in the Caribbean. How often respondents use social media (A) is a variable to be measured, not a test of the sample.

questions.stem: Which of the following sources may yield the MOST accurate and complete data?
questions.explain: Young people can report their own social media use and feelings, and medical professionals can confirm diagnoses and patterns. Together they give the fullest picture; ministers, parents and teachers are further removed.

questions.stem: The ability of Jamaicans to create words like “cookiesha” demonstrates that the Jamaican language is
questions.explain: Creating new words such as “cookiesha” shows that the language keeps growing and changing, which is what “dynamic” means. Symbolic (B) refers to words standing for things and ideas.

questions.stem: Words like “cookiesha”, which are created by sections of the Jamaican population and used informally, are BEST described as
questions.explain: Slang is informal vocabulary created and used by particular groups. Jargon (B) is the technical language of a profession, and register (C) is a level of formality.

questions.stem: Johan mentions dialects of languages other than English spoken in Trinidad. Two of these dialects are
questions.explain: Bhojpuri and Hindustani came to Trinidad with Indian indentured labourers. Garifuna is spoken mainly in Belize and Central America, and Creolese is the Creole of Guyana.

questions.stem: Historically, Trinidad’s linguistic heritage included French Creole. Which other Caribbean countries share this heritage?
questions.explain: French-lexicon Creoles are spoken in Dominica, Haiti and St Lucia, as they once were widely in Trinidad. Jamaica, Barbados and Belize have English-lexicon Creoles, so every other option includes a wrong country.

questions.stem: The MOST appropriate label for languages such as Garifuna, Lokojan, Patamuna, Wapishan and Warao which are spoken in the Caribbean is
questions.explain: These are languages of the region’s first peoples, spoken in places such as Guyana, Belize and Suriname, so they are indigenous languages. They are not dialects of another language or Creoles.

questions.stem: Johan mentioned African languages as part of Jamaica’s linguistic heritage. These include all of the following languages EXCEPT
questions.explain: Akan, Igbo and Koongo are West and Central African languages that helped shape Jamaican Creole. Garifuna (spelt “Garufuna” in the paper) is an Arawakan language of the Garifuna people, now spoken mainly in Belize and Central America.

questions.stem: Fifteen-year-old Tajay refers to his friends as bro and dawg when they hang out. This usage is an illustration of
questions.explain: “Bro” and “dawg” are informal, in-group words used among friends, which is slang. A cliché (B) is an overused phrase, and jargon (C) is specialist vocabulary.

questions.stem: Which of the following BEST describes the maturational characteristic of language?
options: Language must be used in a mature way.
Over time, the meaning of language changes as people use language in different ways.
Over time, the meaning of language changes and language becomes more complex.
questions.explain: The maturational characteristic means a language develops over time: meanings change and the language grows more complex. C describes change only, without the growth in complexity.

questions.stem: If an English-based Creole has words such as ben, beg, and hol, where Standard English uses bend, begged and hold, respectively; which of the following rules is at work in the English-based Creole?
options: No voiced consonant at the end of words
No voiceless consonant at the end of words
No voiced consonant clusters at the end of words
No voiceless consonant clusters at the end of words
questions.explain: Bend, begged and hold each end in two voiced consonants (nd, gd, ld), and the Creole forms drop one of them. A single final voiced consonant remains, as in “ben”, so A is wrong.

questions.stem: In which of the following CARICOM countries does a Creole have official language status?
questions.explain: Haitian Creole (Kreyòl) is an official language of Haiti, alongside French. Guyana, Barbados and Dominica use English as the official language, even though Creoles are widely spoken there.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a challenge faced by the Creole speaker in the learning of English?
options: English is taught as if it is a first language.
Fear of making mistakes while using English.
Similarities between English and other European languages.
Similarities and overlaps in the structure of English and English-based Creoles.
questions.explain: Creole speakers struggle because English is taught as if it were their first language, they fear mistakes, and English and English-based Creoles overlap. Links between English and other European languages do not affect them.

questions.stem: The majority of Trinidadian French Creole speakers are elderly. Which role of language in Caribbean identity is primarily threatened by this situation?
questions.explain: If mainly elderly people speak French Creole, the language is not being passed on to younger generations, so its role in transmitting culture is threatened. Annihilation of culture (A) is not a role of language.

questions.stem: Fatima has been denied a job in a garment factory because she only speaks Guyanese Creolese. Which role of language is MOST likely being breached by the factory?
questions.explain: Refusing someone a job because of the language she speaks is unfair treatment, so the factory breaches the ethical role of language, which concerns fairness and respect. It is not mainly a political (C) or psychological (D) matter.

questions.stem: When Jerome walked into his job interview, he greeted the interview panel with, “Wassup guys?” Which of the following factors did Jerome NOT take into consideration?
questions.explain: “Wassup guys?” is casual language for friends, not for a formal job interview. Jerome ignored the context, which called for a formal register.

questions.stem: The office in charge of disaster preparedness wants to send out an urgent hurricane warning to the entire population using text messaging. Which of the following will present the greatest problem for transmitting the message?
options: Speed of dissemination of the message
Access to devices by the population
Need for technical expertise by receivers
Cost of dissemination for the government
questions.explain: A text-message warning cannot reach people who have no phone, so access to devices is the greatest problem. Text messages are fast (A), easy to read (C) and cheap to send (D).

questions.stem: Which of the following describes the communication process that John should go through to ensure effective communication with his team?
options: Selecting the appropriate channel, transmitting the message and encoding the message
Decoding the message, selecting the appropriate channel and transmitting the message
Selecting the appropriate channel, encoding the message and transmitting the message
Transmitting the message, selecting the appropriate channel and encoding the message
questions.explain: John should choose the channel, encode the message to suit it and then transmit it. A and D put transmitting before encoding, and decoding (B) is done by the receivers, not by John.

questions.stem: What is John’s initial role in the communication process?
questions.explain: John starts the process by turning his ideas into a message, so his first role is encoder. His colleagues are the receivers who will decode it.

questions.stem: Which of the following would be the MOST effective medium to communicate the new strategy to all who need to know?
questions.explain: Face-to-face communication lets John explain the strategy, answer questions and check understanding on the spot. A memo or text (A, C) gives no instant feedback, and social media (B) is too informal for a department policy.

questions.stem: Which of the following would be the MAIN purpose for communicating the new strategy to all who need to know?
options: Allows the receiver to note the message
Explains each person’s role in the implementation
Ensures that the message is transmitted accurately
Gives the main element in the communication process
questions.explain: John wants everyone to understand the strategy and their part in carrying it out, so the main purpose is to explain each person’s role. The other options describe parts of the process, not the reason for communicating.

questions.stem: The BEST way for John to judge whether his colleagues have understood the new strategy is by
questions.explain: Feedback shows the sender whether the message was understood. Assuming understanding (C) or repeating and adding instructions (A, D) does not check what the receivers have taken in.

questions.stem: The behaviour which Sarah’s classmates displayed towards her is BEST described as
questions.explain: Making Sarah doubt her own perception and then telling her she is too sensitive is gaslighting. Propaganda (A) is organised persuasion aimed at a wide audience, and a deep fake (C) is digitally altered media.

questions.stem: If on one occasion, Sarah’s classmates spread stories that she is the most popular girl in the class and that she has won a prestigious scholarship in order to ridicule her, they would be guilty of using
questions.explain: A big lie is a falsehood so bold and exaggerated that people are expected to accept it. Spreading wildly false stories of popularity and a scholarship to mock Sarah fits this. A deep fake (B) needs altered images or video.

questions.stem: What is gaslighting?
options: A psychological technique used to influence an audience’s response
A communication technique used to highlight important concepts only
A psychological manipulation technique aimed at making victims doubt their own perception of reality
A communication strategy that promotes gas as a primary form of energy
questions.explain: Gaslighting is psychological manipulation that makes victims doubt their own memory or perception of reality. A is too general, since many techniques influence an audience, and D takes the word literally.

questions.stem: The strategy of Sarah’s classmates toward her may BEST be classified as
questions.explain: The classmates spread false stories and twist the truth about Sarah, so their strategy is classed as misinformation: false information passed around about her. Fallacies (A) are errors in reasoning, and the misperception (C) is Sarah’s, not theirs.

questions.stem: If a government uses a strategy similar to Sarah’s friends in order to deliberately deceive another government into believing something that is not true, this action may BEST be classified as
questions.explain: Spreading falsehoods is misinformation, and doing it deliberately to deceive another government is disinformation, so both labels apply. Propaganda (C) promotes a cause to a wide public rather than deceiving one government.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the GREATEST advantage to Derek if he incorporates the use of digital media technology in his project?
questions.explain: Digital media lets Derek share his work online, so it can reach a wide audience quickly and easily. Audio, video and links (A, B) are useful features, but wide dissemination is the greatest advantage.

questions.stem: All of the following qualify as digital media technology EXCEPT
questions.explain: A transistor radio is an analogue device that only receives broadcasts. An AV projector, a smart TV and a laptop all handle digital media.

questions.stem:
Which of the following would be the BEST justification for Derek’s use of digital media technology if his target audience consisted of teenagers?
I. Preference for the technology
II. Popularity with target audience
III. Ease of use
questions.explain: Teenagers prefer digital technology, it is popular among them and they find it easy to use. All three reasons justify Derek’s choice.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of interpersonal communication?
options: Talking to a stranger on the bus
Reading a book in a quiet room
Drafting a text message to a friend
questions.explain: Interpersonal communication is a direct exchange between people, such as chatting with a stranger on the bus. Watching, reading or drafting a message alone (A, C, D) involves no exchange yet.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of organizational communication?
options: Sending a message to a group of workers
Talking with a few friends face-to-face
Writing a letter to a family member
questions.explain: Organizational communication takes place within an organization, such as a message sent to a group of workers. Talking with friends (B) and writing to family (C) are interpersonal, and posting on social media (D) is mass communication.

Salt Pond Mornings
Every morning, before the sun open he eye, we was already by the pond.
Mammy with the basket, me with the rake.
Salt shining white like somebody spread sugar over the whole of Sandy Ground.
First we rake, then we pile, then we carry.
Back bending, hand burning, but nobody complaining.
Now look.
Truck and car and dust where the salt used to sleep.
Children passing and don't even turn they head.
Who going tell them?
Who going remember Mammy hand?
I tell them. I tell them every Sunday.
The pond don't forget. Is we who forget.

Original monologue written for this practice paper.

The MAIN purpose of the monologue is to
options: instruct children in how salt is raked and stored
lament the loss of a community tradition and its memory
persuade the government to reopen the salt pond
describe the traffic problems in present-day Sandy Ground
questions.explain: The persona contrasts the busy salt-raking mornings of the past with the present, where "Truck and car and dust" have replaced the salt and children "don't even turn they head". The closing line "Is we who forget" shows the speaker mourning a lost tradition, not instructing, campaigning or reporting on traffic.

Fishers along the Tobago coast report that large mats of sargassum seaweed are reducing their catches. A group of sixth-form students from Sandbox Tree College plans to investigate how sargassum has affected the income of fishers in Charlotteville and Speyside over the last three years.

Which of the following is a PRIMARY source from which the students could gather information?
options: A textbook on Caribbean marine plants
A news article on sargassum on another island
Interviews with fishers who work in Charlotteville
A website summarising global seaweed research
questions.explain: A primary source gives first-hand information from people directly involved. The fishers experienced the drop in catches themselves. The textbook, news article and website report or interpret other people's findings, so they are secondary sources.

questions.explain: Questionnaires are easy to administer to a large number of respondents quickly and produce data that can be compared. Focus groups involve few people, observation cannot show income, and document analysis depends on records that may not exist for individual fishers.

Read the following extract carefully and then answer Items 12–15.

For years, we have treated the bus as the last choice of the traveller who has no other choice. Yet every morning on our main roads, private cars crawl bumper to bumper, most carrying only one person, while schoolchildren wait under the sun at stops with no shelter. If Grenada invested in a scheduled, reliable public bus service, traffic would ease, fuel costs would fall and workers would reach their jobs on time. Other small islands have shown that a well-run timetable can move thousands of people daily. The question is not whether we can afford such a system. The question is whether we can afford to keep going without one.

SOURCE: Adapted from Dana Richardson, "Waiting for the Bus", The Harbour Voice, 2025. Dana Richardson is a transport planner who has advised several island governments in the Eastern Caribbean on public transport.

Which of the following BEST states the main point of the extract?
options: Schoolchildren on the island need bus shelters at every stop.
Private cars are the main cause of air pollution on the island.
Grenada should invest in a reliable public bus service to improve daily life.
Other small islands have better transport systems than Grenada.
questions.explain: The whole extract builds towards the claim that a scheduled, reliable bus service would ease traffic, lower costs and help workers. The bus shelters and other islands are supporting details, and pollution is not mentioned.

Shanice, who was born in Antigua, and her cousin Luis, who recently moved from the Dominican Republic, are waiting in a long line at a government office in St. John's.

Shanice: Boy, the line long, eh? We go be here till evening.

Before the Wind Comes
Good evening, neighbours. Some of you were here for Irma. Some of you were not.

Mangroves are often dismissed as muddy, mosquito-filled swamps. In fact, they are among the hardest-working ecosystems on the island. Their tangled roots trap sediment that would otherwise cloud coral reefs. They provide nurseries where young snapper and lobster grow safely before moving out to sea. During storms, a healthy mangrove belt absorbs the force of waves and protects homes behind it. When mangroves are cleared for marinas and parking lots, all of these services disappear at once: reefs choke, fish stocks fall and the coastline becomes exposed. Protecting what remains of our mangroves on Ambergris Caye is therefore not a luxury for nature lovers. It is a practical investment in the island's food, economy and safety.

SOURCE: Adapted from Marisol Hazel, "The Island's Quiet Guardians", Caribbean Environment Review, 2024. Marisol Hazel is a marine biologist who has studied Caribbean coastal wetlands for fifteen years.

Marinas and parking lots are needed for the island's economy.
Young snapper and lobster grow in mangroves.
Mangroves provide vital services, so protecting them is a practical investment for the island.
questions.explain: A good summary captures the overall claim, not a single detail. The writer lists the services mangroves provide and concludes that protecting them supports food, economy and safety. Option A is the view the writer rejects, and C is only one supporting detail.

The writer opens with the view that mangroves are "muddy, mosquito-filled swamps" MAINLY in order to
options: introduce a common misconception that she will then challenge
persuade readers to avoid visiting Ambergris Caye
show that she agrees with developers
describe the scenery of the island
questions.explain: The writer immediately follows with "In fact", showing that she is setting up a popular but mistaken belief so that she can correct it. This contrast technique makes her argument more striking.

questions.stem:
Read the following extract carefully and then answer Items 12–15.

Mangroves are often dismissed as muddy, mosquito-filled swamps. In fact, they are among the hardest-working ecosystems on the island. Their tangled roots trap sediment that would otherwise cloud coral reefs. They provide nurseries where young snapper and lobster grow safely before moving out to sea. During storms, a healthy mangrove belt absorbs the force of waves and protects homes behind it. When mangroves are cleared for marinas and parking lots, all of these services disappear at once: reefs choke, fish stocks fall and the coastline becomes exposed. Protecting what remains of our mangroves on Ambergris Caye is therefore not a luxury for nature lovers. It is a practical investment in the island's food, economy and safety.

SOURCE: Adapted from Marisol Hazel, "The Island's Quiet Guardians", Caribbean Environment Review, 2024. Marisol Hazel is a marine biologist who has studied Caribbean coastal wetlands for fifteen years.

Which of the following MOST supports the credibility of the extract?
options: The extract uses vivid words such as "choke".
The writer mentions a specific place, Ambergris Caye.
The writer is a marine biologist with fifteen years' experience studying coastal wetlands.
The extract was adapted for a practice paper.
questions.explain: The writer's qualifications and long experience in the exact field she is writing about make her a trustworthy source. Vivid language and place names add interest but do not establish expertise.

In which of the following territories is Papiamentu an official language?
questions.explain: Papiamentu, a Creole with Portuguese, Spanish, Dutch and African influences, is an official language in Aruba, Curaçao and Bonaire. Sint Maarten's main languages are English and Dutch, Suriname's national lingua franca is Sranan Tongo, and Martinique and Guadeloupe use French and French Creole.

questions.stem:

A child born in Aruba learns to speak naturally only after hearing Papiamento, Dutch and Spanish spoken around her. This shows that language is
questions.explain: Language is non-instinctive: humans have the capacity for language but must learn a specific language through exposure in a community. No child is born speaking a particular language.

questions.stem:
Select the most appropriate answer for Items 21–30.

The words "selfie", "unfriend" and "livestream" have recently entered everyday Caribbean speech. This illustrates that language is
questions.explain: A dynamic language changes over time, adding new words to meet new needs (here, social media). Maturational refers to how an individual's language develops as they grow.

questions.stem:
Select the most appropriate answer for Items 21–30.

In many Caribbean Creoles, "thing" is pronounced "ting" and "that" is pronounced "dat". This phonological feature is known as
questions.explain: Th-stopping replaces the "th" sounds of Standard English with the stop consonants /t/ and /d/. It is one of the most widespread phonological features of English-lexicon Caribbean Creoles.

questions.stem:
Select the most appropriate answer for Items 21–30.

The Creole expressions "pretty-pretty" (very pretty) and "fool-fool" (very foolish) illustrate
questions.explain: Reduplication is the repetition of a word to intensify or change its meaning. It is a lexical and grammatical feature found in many Caribbean Creoles and in West African languages.

questions.stem:
Select the most appropriate answer for Items 21–30.

In the sentence "Dem a play cricket", the word "a" marks
questions.explain: In many English-lexicon Creoles, "a" (or "de", "ah") before the verb shows an ongoing action, equivalent to "They are playing cricket". Completed action is marked by "done", and future by "go" or "gwine".

questions.stem:
Select the most appropriate answer for Items 21–30.

When doctors at a hospital discuss a patient's "hypertension" and "BP readings" with one another, they are using
questions.explain: Jargon is the specialised vocabulary of a profession or field. It allows experts to communicate precisely among themselves but may confuse outsiders such as patients.

questions.stem:
Select the most appropriate answer for Items 21–30.

Which of the following factors MOST influences a person's attitude towards Creole in the Caribbean?
options: The person's height and age at school entry
The number of vowels in Creole words
The history of colonialism and the link between language and social class
questions.explain: Attitudes to Creole have been shaped by colonial history, in which European languages were associated with power and education and Creole with enslaved and working-class people. These associations with social class continue to influence attitudes.

questions.stem:
Select the most appropriate answer for Items 21–30.

At a job interview, Kyle sits very close to the interviewer and touches her arm while speaking. Which TWO communicative behaviours are being displayed?
questions.explain: Proxemics is the use of personal space (sitting very close), and haptics is communication through touch (touching her arm). In a formal interview, both may be seen as inappropriate.

questions.stem:
Select the most appropriate answer for Items 21–30.

Arriving thirty minutes late to a business meeting may be interpreted as a lack of respect. This is an aspect of
questions.explain: Chronemics is the study of how time is used and perceived in communication, including punctuality and waiting time. Attitudes to time vary across cultures and contexts.

A youth health network in Dominica is planning a three-month campaign to reduce the consumption of sugary drinks among students aged 12–18. The coordinator, Ms Nadine Arrindell, must first write to the Minister of Public Health requesting funding, then design messages that will reach students in their schools and online.

Ms Arrindell's request to the Minister for funding should be presented in the form of a
options: formal letter accompanied by a proposal
questions.explain: A request to a government minister requires a formal written channel. A formal letter introduces the request, and a proposal sets out the problem, objectives, activities and budget. Memos are for internal use within an organisation.

A youth health network in Dominica is planning a three-month campaign to reduce the consumption of sugary drinks among students aged 12–18. To reach students aged 12–18 MOST effectively, which combination of channels would be BEST for the campaign?
options: School assemblies and short videos on popular social media platforms
questions.explain: Audience profiling shows that teenagers spend much of their time at school and on social media. Combining face-to-face assemblies with short videos on platforms they use places the message where the audience already is.

At a staff meeting, Mr Brooks, the vice principal, explains a new examination timetable. The air-conditioning unit is rattling loudly. Mr Brooks uses terms such as "modular sittings" and "concurrent windows" without explaining them. Several teachers who are already upset about extra supervision duties stop listening. Ms Lake, at the back, nods but later admits she misunderstood the dates.

The rattling air-conditioning unit is an example of
questions.explain: Physical (external) noise is any sound or environmental distraction that interferes with the transmission of the message. Semantic noise relates to meaning and psychological noise to the receiver's emotions or attitudes.

questions.stem:

Ms Lake, at the back, nods but later admits she misunderstood the dates.

Mr Brooks's use of "modular sittings" and "concurrent windows" without explanation creates a

options: A short video posted on a video-sharing platform
questions.explain: Video combines sound, moving images and demonstration, which suits a step-by-step craft process. A video-sharing platform is also easily accessible to young people abroad. Radio and text cannot show the process visually.

questions.stem:

Zara, a CAPE student, is preparing a heritage project about traditional Curaçao Carnival costume-making for an audience of young people living in the diaspora in the Netherlands and the United States.

options: It removes the need for any planning.

It guarantees that every viewer will agree with the content.
It is the only form of communication young people understand.
questions.explain: Digital media overcomes distance, allowing the diaspora audience to view, comment on and share the content at any time. This connects them to their cultural heritage, an example of the global village.

questions.stem:
