options: The content may be copied or used without permission.
The audience can respond with comments.
The content can include images and sound.
The work can reach many people at little cost.
questions.explain: Once posted online, content can easily be downloaded, altered or reused without credit, raising issues of copyright and ownership. The other options are advantages of social media.

questions.stem:
Select the most appropriate answer for Items 44 and 45.

In the communication process, the stage in which the receiver interprets the sender's message is called
questions.explain: Decoding is the receiver's interpretation of the symbols (words, gestures, images) into meaning. Encoding is done by the sender, transmitting is sending through a channel, and feedback is the receiver's response.

questions.stem:
Select the most appropriate answer for Items 44 and 45.

Which model of communication sees both participants as sending and receiving messages at the same time, within a shared context?
questions.explain: The transactional model views communication as simultaneous: participants are communicators who encode and decode at the same time, influenced by context and their fields of experience. Linear models (including Shannon and Weaver and Aristotle's) show one-way flow.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the MAIN reason a researcher should write a focused research question before choosing a data collection method?
options: It determines what information is needed and therefore which methods are suitable.
It allows the researcher to skip the analysis stage.
It guarantees that respondents will answer honestly.
It makes the final report look more academic.
questions.explain: The research question decides what data must be collected, so it guides the choice of method and sample. Option D is tempting because good questions do sound academic, but appearance is not the purpose; the question shapes every later stage of the research process.

questions.stem: A Form 6 student wants to find out how teenagers in Dominica feel about a proposed curfew during Carnival. She asks only the members of her own youth group. Which of the following BEST describes the weakness of this sample?
options: It breaks the rule of informed consent.
It is too large to analyse.
It is not representative of the population.
questions.explain: A convenience sample drawn from one youth group is unlikely to reflect the views of all teenagers on the island, so it is not representative and the findings would be biased. Option A is tempting because ethics matter, but nothing in the scenario suggests consent was ignored; the problem is who was chosen.

questions.stem: Before handing out questionnaires on vaping, a researcher sends home a letter explaining the study and asks parents of students under 18 to sign it. This action reflects the ethical principle of
questions.explain: Explaining the research and obtaining written permission, including from parents of minors, is informed consent. Anonymity is tempting because it is also an ethical principle, but anonymity is about not identifying participants in the findings, not about getting permission.

questions.stem:
Items 4–6: A research team from a community college wants to investigate why fewer young people in the Dutch Caribbean are joining traditional string bands.

Which of the following are primary sources from which the team could gather information?
questions.explain: Interviews conducted by the team produce first-hand data, so they are primary. Newspaper reviews (A) are tempting because they come from the period, but they are reports by someone else interpreting the events, so they are secondary sources.

questions.stem:
Items 4–6: A research team from a community college wants to investigate why fewer young people in the Dutch Caribbean are joining traditional string bands.

Which of the following would be the BEST data collection instrument for probing young people's attitudes towards string band music in depth?
questions.explain: A focus group lets young people discuss and build on each other's views, which is ideal for probing attitudes in depth. A closed questionnaire (D) is tempting because it reaches many people easily, but fixed options limit the depth of explanation the team needs.

questions.stem:
Items 4–6: A research team from a community college wants to investigate why fewer young people in the Dutch Caribbean are joining traditional string bands.

If observation of band rehearsals is used, which of the following could be an ADVANTAGE for the research team?
options: Predicting the results before the study begins
Controlling the behaviour of the musicians
Obtaining large amounts of numerical data quickly
Witnessing natural behaviour directly as it occurs
questions.explain: Observation allows researchers to see what people actually do, as it happens, rather than relying on what they say. Option C is tempting, but large numerical data sets come more readily from questionnaires and surveys.

questions.stem: A questionnaire item reads: "Do you agree that the new bus fares are unfair and that the service is poor?" Which TWO weaknesses does this item show?
options: It is open and too long.
It is vague and uses jargon.
questions.explain: "Do you agree that... unfair" pushes the respondent to agree (leading), and it asks about fares AND service at once (double-barrelled). Option B is tempting because "poor" is a little vague, but the clearest faults are the leading wording and the two questions in one.

questions.stem: A test intended to measure students' listening skills contains mainly questions on spelling. Which of the following BEST describes this test?
questions.explain: Validity is the extent to which a test measures what it aims to measure; a spelling-based test does not measure listening. Option B is tempting because the test might give the same results each time (reliability), but consistent results do not make it measure the right thing.

questions.stem:
"Every serious athlete on the island is drinking PowerCane. Shouldn't you be drinking it too?" (advertisement for a sports drink)
The reasoning in this advertisement is an example of
questions.explain: The advertisement suggests you should drink the product simply because others do, which is the bandwagon fallacy: popularity does not prove quality. Option B is tempting because athletes are mentioned, but no named expert or authority gives evidence.

questions.stem:
A website run by a cruise company states that "cruise tourism brings only benefits to small islands". No author, date or supporting data are given.
Which of the following BEST evaluates the credibility of this information?
options: It is less credible because the producer has a commercial interest and the claim is undated and unsupported.
It is less credible because it is a primary source.
It is credible because it comes from a company with experience in tourism.
It is credible because it is published online.
questions.explain: The company benefits if readers accept the claim (motive), and with no author, date or data, the claim cannot be checked for currency or corroborated. Option C is tempting because experience can suggest authority, but experience does not cancel out a clear commercial bias.

questions.stem:
Our reefs are the island's quiet guardians. They break the force of storm waves, shelter young fish and draw divers from around the world. Yet each year, more of them turn ghostly white.
The phrase "the island's quiet guardians" is an example of
questions.explain: The reefs are directly called guardians (metaphor) and given the human role of protecting (personification). Option D is tempting, but there is no "like" or "as", so it is not a simile, and the claim is not an exaggeration.

questions.stem:
Our reefs are the island's quiet guardians. They break the force of storm waves, shelter young fish and draw divers from around the world. Yet each year, more of them turn ghostly white.
The writer's purpose in this extract is MOST likely to
options: compare Caribbean reefs with reefs elsewhere
entertain readers with a story about divers
explain how fish reproduce in reef habitats
warn readers that the island's protective reefs are being lost
questions.explain: The writer first lists how reefs protect and benefit the island, then uses "Yet" to reveal that they are dying, which creates a warning. Option C is tempting because young fish are mentioned, but that detail supports the main point rather than being the focus.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the MOST complete statement of a writer's main point?
options: Constant social media use is reducing the time Caribbean teenagers spend talking with their families, weakening family relationships.
The effects of social media on teenagers
questions.explain: A main point must be a complete idea that states what the writer claims, not just a topic. Option B is tempting because it is more specific than A, but it is still a phrase that does not say what those effects are.

questions.stem:
Item 14 is based on a short talk read aloud twice by your teacher about preparing for hurricane season.

While the talk is being read, which of the following is the BEST listening practice?
options: Listen only to the first reading and use the second reading to answer.
Note key words and signal words, and wait until the reading is complete before answering.
Begin answering the questions as soon as the main idea becomes clear.
Write down every word the speaker says.
questions.explain: Selective notes on key words and signal words capture the structure without falling behind, and waiting until the end ensures you do not miss information that completes or changes the meaning. Option C is tempting to save time, but the final part of a talk often contains the speaker's real purpose.

questions.stem: In a Module 1 essay, which of the following should the conclusion do?
options: Restate the main point and purpose briefly without new analysis.
Evaluate a source not mentioned in the body paragraphs.
Be longer than the introduction to show depth.
Introduce one final language technique not discussed earlier.
questions.explain: A conclusion sums up the main point, purpose and how the techniques achieve it; it must be shorter than the introduction and contain no new analysis. Options D and B are tempting because they add content, but new points belong in the body, where they can be developed with PEEL.

questions.stem: "The steelpan rang out across the savannah as the morning sun turned the dust to gold." This sentence is MAINLY an example of which form of discourse?
questions.explain: The sentence uses sound and sight imagery to help the reader experience a scene, which is descriptive discourse. Expository is tempting because the sentence states what happened, but it does not explain or inform; its aim is to evoke.

questions.stem: A vlog shows viewers, step by step, how to secure hurricane shutters safely. This vlog is BEST classified as
questions.explain: Instructions and explanations that inform the audience are expository, even when delivered as a vlog. Argumentative is tempting because the topic is safety, but the vlog does not take a position or argue a claim.

questions.stem: An article opens with a story about one family's flooded home, then explains how storm surge forms, and ends by demanding that government build sea defences. Its dominant form and purpose are
options: argumentative, to persuade government to act
questions.explain: The whole extract builds towards a claim and a call to action, so the dominant form is argumentative and the purpose is to persuade. The narrative opening is tempting, but it is a hook that serves the argument.

questions.stem: "The more we tried to save time with the new road, the more time we spent in traffic." This sentence is an example of
questions.explain: A whole statement that seems contradictory but reveals a truth is a paradox. Oxymoron is tempting, but an oxymoron places two contradictory words side by side, as in "deafening silence".

questions.stem: Which of the following is an assumption commonly associated with traditional media such as newspapers and radio?
questions.explain: Traditional media are commonly assumed to be objective, reliable and responsible, though they may face censorship. Susceptibility to conspiracy theories is tempting as a media issue, but it is an assumption usually made about new media.

questions.stem: A research team needs to find out both how many fishermen have changed fishing grounds since sargassum increased and why they did so. Which research design is MOST appropriate?
questions.explain: "How many" requires quantitative data and "why" requires qualitative data, so mixed methods (for example, questionnaires plus interviews) fit best. A case study is tempting for depth, but one case cannot show how many fishermen changed.

questions.stem: A student writes in a formal report: "At the end of the day, the council needs to think outside the box." The expressions "at the end of the day" and "think outside the box" are BEST described as
questions.explain: Overused phrases that have lost their force are clichés and weaken formal writing. Jargon is tempting, but jargon is the specialised vocabulary of a profession, not worn-out everyday phrases.

questions.stem: Fourteen-year-old Javon creates the word "phonezombie" for a classmate who never looks up from his phone, and soon the whole form uses it. This demonstrates that language is
questions.explain: A new word entering a group's everyday use shows that language changes and grows: it is dynamic. "Arbitrary" is tempting because any new word is arbitrary, but the point of the item is the creation and spread of a new form, which is change.

questions.stem: Shania refers to her friends as "fam" and "bestie" when they lime after school. This usage is an illustration of
questions.explain: Very informal, in-group words used among friends are slang. Jargon is tempting, but jargon is the specialised vocabulary of a profession or activity, not friendly in-group talk.

questions.stem: In which of the following countries does a Creole have official language status alongside a European language?
questions.explain: Haiti recognises both Haitian Creole and French as official languages. Saint Lucia is tempting because Kwéyòl is widely spoken there, but its official language is English.

questions.stem: Which group of Caribbean territories shares a French-lexified Creole heritage?
questions.explain: Kwéyòl in Dominica and Saint Lucia and Haitian Creole all take most of their vocabulary from French. Aruba, Curaçao and Bonaire are tempting because they are not English-speaking, but their Papiamentu draws mainly on Portuguese and Spanish.

questions.stem: A speaker of an English-based Creole says "spector" for "inspector" and "gainst" for "against". Which phonological process is at work?
questions.explain: Colloquial aphesis is the loss of an unstressed sound or syllable at the beginning of a word. Cluster reduction is tempting because sounds are lost, but cluster reduction drops a consonant at the END of a word, as in "han'" for "hand".

questions.stem: The pronunciations "aks" for "ask" and "cripsy" for "crispy" are examples of
questions.explain: In metathesis, sounds swap places in a word. Epenthesis is tempting, but epenthesis ADDS a sound, as in "sinake" for "snake"; nothing is added here.

questions.stem:
"Di teacher does give we plenty homework."

In the sentence above, "does" functions as a
options: pre-verbal particle marker showing habitual action
questions.explain: "Does" comes systematically before the verb "give" to show that the action happens regularly: a habitual pre-verbal particle marker. "Past tense" is tempting, but past time in many Caribbean Creoles is marked by "did", "ben" or "en".

questions.stem: The sentences "Mi siki" (Jamaican) and "Mwen malad" (Kwéyòl), both meaning "I am sick", illustrate which feature of Caribbean Creole grammar?
options: Predicative use of adjectives without a form of "be"
questions.explain: The adjective itself acts as the predicate with no copula, a structure patterned on West African sources. Subject-verb agreement is tempting, but there is no verb to agree with; that is the point.

questions.stem:
At the bank, Ms. Richardson tells a client, "Your loan application has been approved." Turning to her colleague, she adds, "Girl, dat man face light up like Christmas!"

Ms. Richardson's change of variety is BEST described as
questions.explain: She moves between Standard English and Creole within a conversation to suit two different audiences: code-switching. Diglossia is tempting, but it describes the separate functions of two varieties in a whole community, not one speaker's moves.

questions.stem: A child whose first language is an English-based Creole is taught entirely in Standard English. Which of the following is NOT a challenge this child is likely to face?
options: Confusion caused by overlaps between Creole and English vocabulary
Fear of making mistakes because of negative attitudes to Creole
Similarities between English and other European languages
Believing she already speaks English because English is official
questions.explain: Similarities between English and other European languages, such as French, do not affect a Creole speaker learning English. The overlap option is tempting to choose, but overlaps between Creole and English are a real and well-known challenge.

questions.stem:
During a job interview at a Port of Spain hotel, Devon leans back, puts his feet on the chair rung and greets the panel with "Wha' happenin', boss?"

Which factor did Devon FAIL to consider in choosing his register?
options: The language of the hotel's guests
questions.explain: A job interview is a formal context calling for a formal register and an upright posture. "Channel" is tempting, but face-to-face speech was appropriate; it was his register and body language that ignored the context.

questions.stem:
"Ever since my teacher told me Creole would keep me from getting a job, I feel ashamed when I use it," Nadia admits.

Nadia's attitude and the factor that produced it are BEST described as
options: admiration, produced by history and society
questions.explain: "Ashamed" signals embarrassment, and the source is a teacher's comment: education. Socialisation is tempting, but socialisation refers to family and community, not schooling.

questions.stem: At a funeral in Trinidad and Tobago, most mourners wear white. This use of colour to convey a cultural message is called
questions.explain: Chromatics is the use of colour to convey meanings, emotions or cultural messages. Proxemics is tempting as another "-emics" term, but it refers to the use of space.

questions.stem: A teenager uses the username "@CastriesFinest" and a Saint Lucian flag as her profile picture. These are BEST described as
questions.explain: A digital identifier is any digital representation, such as a name, icon or picture, used to uniquely identify a person. Idiomatic expressions are tempting because the name carries meaning, but idioms are figurative sayings like "cut your eye".

questions.stem: "Mi foot a hurt mi" uses "foot" to mean the whole leg. This is an example of
questions.explain: An English word has taken on a different meaning in Creole: semantic shift, a lexical feature. The other options are phonological processes about sounds, but the pronunciation of "foot" has not changed, only its meaning.

questions.stem: Which theory of creole origin argues that children who heard only an unstable pidgin used an inborn human capacity for language to create a full creole grammar?
questions.explain: The bioprogram hypothesis explains creole grammar through children's innate language ability. Monogenesis is tempting because it is also a theory of origin, but it traces creoles to a single early Portuguese-based pidgin, not to an inborn capacity.

questions.stem: Similarities between English-lexified and French-lexified creoles are explained by some linguists as the result of one ancestral pidgin whose vocabulary was later replaced word by word. This replacement process is called
questions.explain: Relexification is the replacement of a language's vocabulary while its grammar remains, a key idea in monogenesis. Language shift is tempting, but it describes a community abandoning one language for another, not swapping vocabulary within one.

questions.stem: The MOST appropriate label for languages such as Garifuna, Lokono, Wapishana and Warao, which are spoken in the Caribbean region, is
questions.explain: These languages were born in the region and its mainland rim before European colonisation, so they are indigenous languages. Creole languages is tempting because they are Caribbean, but creoles arose later from contact situations such as the plantation.

questions.stem: Caribbean Hindustani and Bhojpuri, still heard in parts of Trinidad, Guyana and Suriname, are BEST described as
options: dialects of Hindi brought by indentured labourers
questions.explain: The syllabus describes Hindustani and Bhojpuri as dialects of Hindi; they arrived with Indian indentured labourers after emancipation. Indigenous languages is tempting because they have long been in the region, but they were brought from Asia, not born here.

questions.stem: The majority of speakers of a French Creole in one territory are elderly, and few children are learning it. Which role of language in Caribbean identity is MOST threatened?
questions.explain: When a language is not passed to children, the culture it carries cannot be transmitted across generations. Building of community is tempting, but the key problem is the break between generations.

questions.stem: A hotel refuses to employ a qualified applicant only because she speaks with a strong Creole accent, although the post involves no contact with guests. Which role of language is MOST likely being breached?
questions.explain: Unfair treatment and discrimination because of the way someone speaks is an ethical issue. Psychological is tempting because the applicant may lose confidence, but the hotel's action itself breaches fairness.

questions.stem: During a conversation with a visiting American, a straw-market vendor in Nassau gradually adjusts her speech to sound more like the visitor's. This is an example of
questions.explain: Adjusting one's speech to become more like the listener's is convergence. Divergence is tempting because it is the paired term, but divergence emphasises differences rather than reducing them.

questions.stem: A government plans to send an urgent hurricane warning to the whole population by text message. Which of the following is likely to present the GREATEST problem?
options: Cost of each message to the government
Access to devices by the population
questions.explain: Not everyone has a mobile phone, signal or power, so access is the greatest obstacle to reaching the whole population. Cost is tempting, but text messages are relatively cheap compared with the risk of people not receiving the warning.

questions.stem: During a tense meeting, a student gives his teacher a long, hard stare instead of replying. This non-verbal behaviour is BEST classified as
questions.explain: Oculesics is the study of eye behaviour, such as staring, gaze and eye contact. Artefacts is tempting as another non-verbal code, but it refers to objects, clothing and appearance.

questions.stem: A candidate applying for a bank job uses the email address "partyqueen_sxm@..." This is BEST described as
questions.explain: A digital identifier, such as an email address or username, should suit the context; a party nickname is inappropriate for a formal job application. Code-mixing is tempting because it involves language choice, but it refers to blending two languages in one utterance.

questions.stem: "Over time, the meaning of language changes and language becomes more complex." This statement BEST describes which characteristic of language?
questions.explain: Growth in complexity over time is the maturational characteristic. Non-instinctive is tempting because it is about acquisition, but it refers to language being learned from a community rather than inherited.

questions.stem: The Creole phrase "eye-water" (tears) is an example of which vocabulary feature?
questions.explain: "Eye-water" shows its meaning on the surface: water from the eye. Hypercorrection is tempting as another named feature, but it is a phonological process, such as adding /h/ in "hegg".

questions.stem: Ms. Hodge, Head of the Business Department at a Jamaican secondary school, must explain a new coursework late-submission policy to her department. Which sequence describes what she should do to communicate effectively?
options: Decode the message, select the channel, transmit the message
Select the channel, transmit the message, encode the message
Transmit the message, encode the message, select the channel
Encode the message, select the appropriate channel, transmit the message
questions.explain: The sender first encodes the idea into words, then chooses a suitable channel and transmits the message. Option B is tempting because channel choice is important, but a message cannot be sent before it has been encoded; decoding is the receiver's task, not the sender's.

questions.stem: What is the BEST way for Ms. Hodge to judge whether her colleagues have understood the new policy?
options: Assuming they understood because nobody objected
questions.explain: Feedback is the only way a sender can verify that a message was understood; without it, communication cannot be confirmed as complete. Restating the policy (A) may help, but it still gives her no evidence of understanding, and silence (B) is not proof.

questions.stem: During a face-to-face meeting, a manager notices a worker frowning while she explains a new roster, so she rephrases her point mid-sentence. Which model of communication BEST describes this exchange?
questions.explain: Both people are sending and receiving messages at the same time and adjusting to each other, which is the transactional model. Interactive (B) is tempting, but it describes turn-taking, where feedback comes only after the sender has finished.

questions.stem: A notice says, "Frederick Street closes to traffic at 6 p.m." It is posted on the morning of the Carnival parade, for drivers, to prevent traffic jams. The details about when, for whom and why the notice was posted describe its
questions.explain: Context is where, when, to whom and why a message is sent. The content (A) is the actual words, "Frederick Street closes to traffic at 6 p.m.", not the circumstances around them.

questions.stem: The disaster management office plans to send an urgent hurricane warning to the entire population of St. Vincent and the Grenadines by text message only. Which of the following presents the GREATEST problem for this plan?
options: Access to mobile devices across the population
questions.explain: Not everyone owns a phone or has a working network after a storm, so access is the greatest barrier to reaching the entire population. Speed (A) is actually an advantage of text messaging, not a problem.

questions.stem: Jerome greets an interview panel at a hotel in Negril with "Wassup, guys?" Which factor did Jerome FAIL to consider?
questions.explain: A job interview is a formal context that requires a formal register, so Jerome misjudged the context. Gender (B) is tempting because "guys" is not gender sensitive, but the main error is using a casual greeting in a formal situation.

questions.stem: A rumour that the principal will be transferred spreads quickly through the staff room and WhatsApp chats before any official announcement. This is an example of
questions.explain: Unofficial, unconfirmed information passed informally is the grapevine. It may travel between peers, which makes horizontal communication (B) tempting, but horizontal communication refers to formal coordination between people at the same level.

questions.stem: A clinic wants to remind residents over 70, many with limited schooling and no smartphones, about free eye tests. Which medium is MOST suitable?
options: A spoken announcement at church and community centres, with large-print flyers
questions.explain: The audience profile (age, educational background, limited access) points to spoken and large-print media where these residents already gather. The QR code (D) and Instagram (A) depend on smartphones the audience does not have.

questions.stem: At a parents' meeting, a guest speaker addresses the audience only as "gentlemen" and assumes all the nurses in the room are women. Which barrier is MOST evident?
questions.explain: Gender-exclusive language and assumptions about roles create a gender barrier; the repair is gender sensitive language such as "everyone" and "nurses". Semantic (D) is tempting because it involves word choice, but the problem is exclusion by gender, not confusing vocabulary.

questions.stem: A Spanish-speaking family in Belmopan cannot understand an English-only flyer about a dengue outbreak. Which repair BEST addresses this barrier?
options: Translating the flyer into Spanish and adding clear pictures
Repeating the English flyer on social media
Printing the flyer in larger type
Posting the flyer in more locations
questions.explain: The barrier is semantic (language), so the repair must change the language: translation, supported by pictures. Posting more copies (D) or using social media (C) spreads the same English message without making it understandable.

questions.stem: A video circulates in which a public figure's face has been digitally placed on another person's body so that he appears to say something he never said. This is BEST described as
questions.explain: A video in which a person's face or body is digitally altered to make them appear to be someone else is a deepfake. A big lie (A) is a gross, repeated distortion of facts used as propaganda, which does not depend on altered video.

questions.stem: A group vandalises its own campaign posters and then publicly blames a rival group to win public sympathy. This tactic is BEST described as
questions.explain: A harmful action designed to look as though someone else carried it out is a false flag. Misinformation (A) is false information shared without intent to deceive, but this act is deliberate.

questions.stem: "Hurricane season starts in two weeks: the time to prepare is now." Which rhetorical appeal does this line MAINLY use?
questions.explain: The line uses timeliness, the urgency of the approaching season, which is kairos. Logos (B) is tempting because a date is a fact, but the persuasive force comes from the timing, not from reasoning or evidence.

questions.stem: A Carnival fete advert says: "Feel the soca in your soul! Half-price tickets until Wednesday, and free shuttles so nobody drinks and drives." Which appeals are combined?
questions.explain: "Feel the soca in your soul" stirs excitement (pathos), "until Wednesday" uses timing (kairos), and cheap tickets and free shuttles give practical reasons (logos). There is no credible speaker or authority, so options with ethos (B, C) are incorrect.

questions.stem: Which of the following qualifies as digital media technology that could enhance a presentation to school administrators?
options: A Canva slideshow displayed on a smart TV
questions.explain: Presentation software on a smart TV is digital media technology that is attractive, easy to use and plays back instantly. A transistor radio (A) is an analogue device and is not accepted as digital media technology unless it is specified as digital.

questions.stem: "Who says what, in which channel, to whom, with what effect?" This question summarises
questions.explain: Lasswell's model frames communication as five questions ending with the effect on the audience. Berlo's SMCR model is tempting because it is also linear, but it is built around source, message, channel and receiver factors, not the five questions.

questions.stem: In Berlo's SMCR model, the "channel" refers to
options: the noise that interferes with a message
the five senses through which a message is received
the context in which communication occurs
questions.explain: Berlo describes channels as the senses: hearing, seeing, touching, smelling and tasting. Feedback is tempting, but the SMCR model, like other linear models, does not include feedback.

questions.stem: At a hotel, the head of the accounts department emails a junior chef in the kitchen directly about a missing invoice. This is an example of
questions.explain: The message crosses both departments and levels of the hierarchy, which is diagonal (cross-channel) communication. Horizontal is tempting because two departments are involved, but horizontal communication is between people at the same level.

questions.stem: "Those who want a curfew for minors want to lock all young people indoors forever." This statement is an example of which fallacy?
questions.explain: The speaker exaggerates and misrepresents the opposing view to make it easier to attack: a strawman. Red herring is tempting, but a red herring changes the subject rather than distorting the opponent's position.

questions.stem: "Either we build the new cruise pier or the island's economy will collapse." This statement is BEST described as
questions.explain: Only two options are offered when others exist, which is the either/or fallacy (false dilemma). Faulty causation is tempting because the economy is mentioned, but the error is the false choice, not a mistaken cause.

questions.stem: A student says "I'm fine, Miss" in a flat voice while avoiding eye contact and slumping in her chair. Her non-verbal cues are MAINLY
questions.explain: Her voice, eyes and posture send a message opposite to her words, so they contradict them. Reinforcing is tempting, but reinforcing cues match and strengthen the words.

questions.stem: A friend tells you about her parents' divorce. You listen patiently, nod and say, "That sounds really hard." You are MAINLY using
questions.explain: Listening to offer emotional and moral support is empathic listening. Comprehensive listening is tempting because you do understand her, but your main purpose is support.

questions.stem: A Minister reads a carefully worded statement on a new immigration policy at a press conference. This mode of delivery is
questions.explain: Reading aloud from a full script is manuscript delivery, chosen when exact wording matters. Extemporaneous is tempting for a prepared talk, but extemporaneous speakers use brief notes, not a full script.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the MOST serious weakness in a presenter's visual aids?
options: Using one main idea per slide
Reading aloud a slide filled with a full page of text
Using large dark font on a pale background
questions.explain: A text-heavy slide read aloud overloads the audience and makes the speaker redundant. The other options are principles of effective design, not weaknesses.

questions.stem: Which of the following sentences is written in the correct style for minutes of a meeting?
options: "The Treasurer reported that the car wash had made a profit."
"Malik says the car wash made loads of money!"
"We will discuss the car wash at the next meeting."
"I think the car wash was a great success."
questions.explain: Minutes use reported speech, the past tense and the third person, and they stay objective. The first option is tempting because it records the report, but it uses the present tense and slang.

questions.stem: A document sent to members before a meeting, listing apologies, confirmation of minutes, matters arising and items of business in order, is
questions.explain: An agenda sets out, in order, the items to be discussed. A notice is tempting because it is also sent before the meeting, but a notice mainly announces the date, time and venue.

questions.stem: Which of the following BEST describes a person's digital footprint?
options: The speed of a person's internet connection
The number of devices a person owns
The permanent trail of content a person posts, shares and interacts with online
questions.explain: A digital footprint is the lasting record of a person's online activity, which others, including employers, may see. A professional email address is tempting because it is part of an online identity, but it is a digital identifier, not the whole footprint.

questions.stem: A student moves her strongest argument to the final paragraph and deletes a point that does not support her thesis. At which stage of the writing process is she working?
questions.explain: Revising improves content and organisation, such as reordering and cutting points. Proofreading is tempting because it is also a checking stage, but it deals only with surface errors such as spelling and punctuation.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes Paper 032?
options: Three compulsory questions covering the three Modules, based on a central stimulus
Three optional questions on three different stimuli
Two essays chosen from five topics
One long essay on the student's own topic
questions.explain: The regulations state three compulsory questions, covering the three Modules and based on a central stimulus. Option B is tempting because it mentions three questions, but they are compulsory and share one stimulus.

questions.stem: What may a candidate bring into Paper 032?
options: One sheet of notes plus a printed guide
A single sheet of double-sided A4 paper with no more than 10 points related to the topic of the response
questions.explain: For the 2027 examination, only a single double-sided A4 sheet with no more than 10 points, and nothing else, is permitted. Option C looks equivalent because the total is still 10 points, but only one sheet is allowed.

questions.stem: What are the topic and intended audience for 2027?
questions.explain: 2027 is non-communicable diseases in children, for parents. Option B is tempting because its audience is also parents, but cyberbullying is the 2030 topic.

questions.stem: A candidate answers Q1(a) with: "Literacy and cost." Based on the specimen mark scheme, what is this likely to earn out of 4?
questions.explain: Two challenges identified but not explained earn 1 mark; 2 marks each require clear explanation. Option A is too harsh, because correct identification is still credited.

questions.stem: Which answer best fits: "Justify ONE appropriate traditional medium, other than the printed medium, for informing elderly homeowners in a rural village about free roof inspections"?
options: "A newspaper advert, because it reaches many readers."
"A flyer, because people can keep it."
"Radio, because it is cheap to own, reaches rural districts and can repeat the message several times a day while older listeners go about their chores."
questions.explain: Radio is traditional, not print, and the answer gives reasons linked to the target group. Options A and B are print, which the question excludes, and Instagram is digital rather than traditional.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest comment on a local source of information about a children's health screening programme?
options: "Parents could consult the nurse at their community clinic, who is trained and works directly with the screening programme, so her information is accurate and current."
"A friend's group chat, because it is fast."
questions.explain: It names a credible local source and explains its authority and currency, earning the full 2 marks. Option C is fast but unreliable, and options B and D are identification without comment.

questions.stem:
"Homeowners are advised that applications for the shutter subsidy close on 30 April. Proof of ownership must be submitted."

Which answer to "Explain the dialectal variety and register used" earns full marks?
options: "Standard English, because it is the official variety used by government; formal register, because the notice is official and concerns a serious financial matter."
questions.explain: Each feature is identified and explained, earning 1 + 1 twice. Option A identifies both correctly but explains neither, so it earns only 1 mark.

questions.stem: "A strap in time saves the roof." Which literary technique does this slogan use?
questions.explain: It alludes to the proverb "A stitch in time saves nine", suggesting early action prevents greater damage. It is not a rhetorical question, since it is a statement, not a question.

questions.stem: How is Question 3(a), the 200–250 word piece, marked in the specimen?
options: Out of 25, in bands, for creativity, organisation and expression
Out of 15, for purpose, audience and context only
questions.explain: The piece is marked out of 25 in bands considering creativity, organisation and expression. Option D describes the justification, which is the separate 15-mark part.

questions.stem: Which sentence in a justification names the CONTEXT of communication?
options: "It would be published in the home section of a weekend newspaper in May."
"The purpose is to persuade homeowners to secure their roofs."
"The intended audience is homeowners in hillside districts."
questions.explain: Context means where and how the piece appears in the real world. Option B is tempting, but "about hurricanes" is content, not context.

questions.stem: "With hurricane season six weeks away, there has never been a better moment to check your roof." Which rhetorical appeal is this?
questions.explain: Kairos appeals to timeliness: why act now. Logos may seem possible because a reason is given, but the reason rests on timing rather than evidence.

questions.stem: A student has 15 minutes left. Section B's piece is finished, but there is no justification. What should the student do FIRST?
options: Write the 50–100 word justification of purpose, intended audience and context
questions.explain: The justification is worth 15 marks, so securing it is the priority. Polishing the opening (A) feels productive but cannot recover 15 missing marks.

questions.stem: A student wants to research the effect of the tourism season on young people in The Bahamas. Which is the BEST research question?
options: Is tourism good or bad for the island?
How does part-time work during the cruise season affect the school attendance of Form 5 students in Nassau?
Why do tourists love The Bahamas so much?

questions.stem:
Jayden is researching how students at his school travel to school. Answer each quick question.

All 520 students at the school are the...
questions.explain: The population is the whole group you want to know about. The sample is the smaller group you actually ask.

questions.stem: Jayden puts every student's name in a box and draws 50. This is...
questions.explain: Every student had an equal chance of being drawn, which is the definition of random sampling.

questions.stem: He only asks students waiting at the bus stop. Why is this a problem?
options: Students who walk or are driven are left out, so the sample is biased.
questions.explain: The sample would over-represent bus users and give a misleading picture of how the whole school travels.

questions.stem: He chooses 10 students from each form level, Form 1 to Form 5. This is...
questions.explain: He divided the population into groups (form levels) and chose from each, which is stratified sampling.

questions.stem: To understand the school's transport policy, he interviews the deputy principal. This is...
questions.explain: He chose the deputy principal on purpose because of her special knowledge. That is purposive sampling.

questions.stem:
A youth council in Barbados wants to find out how many secondary students have stopped using public buses since fares rose, and the reasons behind their decisions. It has six weeks and a small team.

Which research design is MOST suitable, and why?
options: A case study of one student who no longer takes the bus.
Qualitative interviews only, with the bus drivers.
Mixed methods: a questionnaire to a sample of students to count how many have stopped, followed by focus groups to explore their reasons.
An experiment in which fares are lowered for one school to see what happens.

questions.stem:
A group of Form 6 students is researching vaping among teenagers in the Cayman Islands. Sort each action.

Is this research action ethical?

They send home consent forms for parents of participants under 18.
questions.explain: Minors need parental consent. This is exactly right.

questions.stem:
Is this research action ethical?

They post a funny screenshot of one student's answers in the class group chat.
questions.explain: This breaks confidentiality and could cause real embarrassment or harm.

questions.stem:
Is this research action ethical?

Questionnaires do not ask for names.
questions.explain: This protects anonymity, which also encourages honest answers on a sensitive topic.

questions.stem:
Is this research action ethical?

They tell participants they can skip any question or stop at any time.
questions.explain: This respects the right to withdraw.

questions.stem:
Is this research action ethical?

They secretly record conversations in the bathroom.
questions.explain: Covert recording without consent invades privacy and breaks the principle of informed consent.

questions.stem:
Is this research action ethical?

They change a few answers so the results look more dramatic.
questions.explain: Falsifying data is dishonest and destroys the reliability of the whole study.

questions.stem:
Is this research action ethical?

They ask the principal for permission before handing out questionnaires at school.
questions.explain: Getting permission from those responsible for the premises is good practice.

questions.topic: Sources and Methods of Data Collection
questions.stem:
Shania is researching how the 2017 hurricanes affected fishing families in Dominica. Sort her sources.

What type of source is each item?

Her recorded interview with a fisherman from Scotts Head.
questions.explain: She collected this first-hand, so it is primary.

questions.topic: Sources and Methods of Data Collection
questions.stem:
What type of source is each item?

Photographs a fisherman took of his damaged boat.
questions.explain: Original images created at the time of the event are primary.

questions.topic: Sources and Methods of Data Collection
questions.stem:
What type of source is each item?

A magazine feature analysing the recovery of the fishing industry.
questions.explain: The writer interprets and reports on other people's information, so it is secondary.

questions.topic: Sources and Methods of Data Collection
questions.stem:
What type of source is each item?

An online encyclopedia entry on Atlantic hurricanes.
questions.explain: Encyclopedias summarise many sources, so they are tertiary.

questions.topic: Sources and Methods of Data Collection
questions.stem:
What type of source is each item?

A documentary that combines interviews with a narrator's commentary.
questions.explain: The documentary interprets primary material for an audience, so it is secondary.

questions.topic: Sources and Methods of Data Collection
questions.stem:
What type of source is each item?

Her own questionnaire completed by 30 fishing households.
questions.explain: Data she collected herself is primary.

questions.topic: Sources and Methods of Data Collection
questions.stem:
What type of source is each item?

A dictionary of Caribbean English used to define "seine".
questions.explain: Dictionaries are reference collections, so they are tertiary.

questions.topic: Sources and Methods of Data Collection
questions.stem:
Two Form 6 students are planning research. Study A: garbage disposal practices in your community (needs reliable sources). Study B: experiences of COVID-19 patients in Trinidad and Tobago (needs valid sources). Decide whether each source should be used or rejected.

Should the researcher use this source?

Study A: residents who live in the community
questions.explain: They experience the disposal practices directly, so they are a reliable source.

questions.topic: Sources and Methods of Data Collection
questions.stem:
Should the researcher use this source?

Study A: the community's sanitation workers
questions.explain: They collect the garbage and know the volumes and types of waste: reliable.

questions.topic: Sources and Methods of Data Collection
questions.stem:
Should the researcher use this source?

Study A: an internet article on garbage disposal
questions.explain: A general secondary source that does not speak to your community.

questions.topic: Sources and Methods of Data Collection
questions.stem:
Should the researcher use this source?

Study A: people from the next community
questions.explain: Their collection days and practices may differ, so they are not representative.

questions.topic: Sources and Methods of Data Collection
questions.stem:
Should the researcher use this source?

Study B: Couva Hospital records, March to May 2020
questions.explain: Right territory, right disease, right time: valid.

questions.topic: Sources and Methods of Data Collection
questions.stem:
Should the researcher use this source?

Study B: interviews with COVID-19 survivors in Trinidad and Tobago

Hyperlinks connect one article to dozens of others.

questions.stem:

questions.stem:

Assumed to practise responsible reporting, though it may face censorship.

Readers comment, share and reply within seconds.

questions.topic: Main Point, Author's Purpose and Reading Strategies
questions.stem:
Every evening across the island, families gather around the dinner table, but many are no longer really together. Parents scroll through work emails while children watch videos with earphones in.

Grandparents, who once told stories of the old salt-pond days, now find that no one is listening. Their knowledge, passed down orally for generations, risks being lost.

Teachers report that some students struggle to hold a conversation, maintain eye contact or read the emotions on a classmate's face.

Which statement BEST expresses the main point of this extract?
options: Heavy use of personal devices is weakening face-to-face communication across generations, in families and in schools.
Families eat dinner together every evening.
Grandparents tell stories about the salt ponds.

questions.topic: Main Point, Author's Purpose and Reading Strategies
questions.stem:
Every morning the treadmill and I renew our quarrel. Its belt seems to be moving me backwards as I begrudgingly barrel forward, staring at an outdated screen that glows like burning coals. The brochure promised that running indoors would leave me somehow connected to nature. Perhaps it meant one of nature's cruel parts.

questions.topic: Forms of Discourse, Modes of Reading and Usage
questions.stem:

"The morning I sat my first CAPE exam, I woke at four, prayed, ate nothing, and walked the long way to school."
questions.explain: A personal sequence of past events: a narrative journal-style account.

"The old salt pond on Grand Turk lay flat and silver under the noon sun, its edges crusted white and smelling faintly of sea and mud."
questions.explain: Sight, touch and smell images with no argument and no story: descriptive.

questions.topic: Forms of Discourse, Modes of Reading and Usage

"Her market stall was a riot of colour: scarlet peppers, golden mangoes and bunches of green thyme piled high."
questions.explain: Vivid sensory detail to help the reader see the stall: descriptive.

questions.topic: Forms of Discourse, Modes of Reading and Usage
questions.stem:

"To register for the scholarship, first download the form, then attach your transcript, and finally submit it before 30 June."
questions.explain: Step-by-step instructions with sequence words: expository.

Last August, fifteen-year-old Dario cycled to Willemstad every morning, a hot, dusty ride along a road with no shoulder and trucks roaring past within an arm's length.

Road safety data from many countries show that separated cycle lanes reduce injuries. Painted lines cost little; a protective kerb costs more but saves lives.

Our island cannot keep asking children to gamble with their lives to get to summer jobs. The Ministry must build a protected cycle lane on this route before next summer.

Which statement BEST identifies the dominant form of this extract and the writer's purpose?
options: It is mainly argumentative/persuasive; the writer's purpose is to persuade the Ministry to build a protected cycle lane, using a narrative hook and expository evidence to support the claim.
It is mainly expository; the writer's purpose is to explain how cycle lanes are built.
It is mainly narrative; the writer's purpose is to entertain readers with Dario's story.
It is mainly descriptive; the writer's purpose is to describe the road to Willemstad.

This supports the writer's purpose of criticizing how cruise tourism profits are distributed.
The writer is clearly against tourism and wants it banned.
