questions.stem: A student is writing about rising sea levels around the Turks and Caicos Islands. Which source is MOST credible for the essay?
options: A 1998 encyclopaedia entry on Caribbean geography
A hotel website promoting its beachfront rooms
A viral video in which a fisherman says the sea "has never changed"
A 2024 report by a regional climate research centre, with named scientists and data tables

questions.stem:
You are writing a Paper 2 essay on the credibility of information about climate change in the Caribbean. You find four sources. For each, note the medium and how it affects credibility.

Source 1: A Facebook post by a Form 6 student: "Rising sea levels are a hoax made up by scientists to get government money. My uncle says the sea hasn't changed in 40 years."

What medium is this?
options: Social media post from a private citizen

questions.stem: Would you cite this in your essay as credible information about climate change?
options: No. It is not credible. You might mention it as an example of a conspiracy theory, but it is not evidence.
Yes, because it is on social media, so many people have seen it.

questions.stem:
Source 2: A peer-reviewed article in the Caribbean Journal of Marine Science titled "Sea Level Rise in the Dutch Caribbean: Data from 1980–2025" by Dr. Amara Osei, a university researcher, and three other marine scientists. The abstract cites 47 studies and includes a data table and statistical analysis.

What medium is this?
options: Academic journal article, a traditional media format with gatekeeping

questions.stem: How does the medium affect credibility?
options: The journal had editors and peer reviewers who checked the science before it was published. The authors are named experts. The article cites 47 other studies, so it is corroborated.
All journal articles are true because they are in journals.

questions.stem:
Source 3: A YouTube video titled "The TRUTH About Climate Change!!!" posted by a channel called "Real Facts Now" with 3 million subscribers. The creator is not named. The video claims the same thing as your Source 1 (the hoax), but with dramatic music and edited clips from news reports.

What medium is this?
options: New media (social video) with no transparent creator or gatekeeping

questions.stem: Why would this be unreliable for your essay?
options: It is on YouTube, so it must be wrong.
The creator is anonymous, there is no fact-checking, and the claims contradict published science. You cannot cite it as evidence.

questions.stem:
Source 4: An article from The Guardian (a reputable international newspaper) by a named journalist, reporting on a recent study from the University of Cambridge on Caribbean coastal erosion. The article quotes the lead researcher, links to the original study, and includes interviews with two residents whose homes have been affected.

For your essay, you would cite this as:
options: Not credible because it is not from an academic journal.
Largely credible. It is a named journalist in an established traditional medium (newspaper). The source is named, quotes are from real people, and the original research is linked.

questions.stem:
The student council is researching the reasons for the decline in student participation in co-curricular activities. Answer each question as you would in Paper 1.

The most appropriate data collection method for this study is...
questions.explain: The research needs a wide cross-section of the student population, and questionnaires allow the largest number of participants. Observation and focus groups reach smaller groups; document research is a secondary source.

questions.stem: One weakness of conducting interviews as a data collection method is...
options: they capture verbal and non-verbal language
the limited size of the interviewee population
questions.explain: Interviews limit the sample size: you cannot reach as wide a cross-section of students as with a questionnaire. Flexibility and capturing non-verbal language are strengths.

questions.stem: The most efficient method of administering the questionnaire is...
questions.explain: Getting responses back is a key difficulty with questionnaires. Face-to-face administration lets you distribute and collect on the spot, which maximises the response rate.

questions.stem: The research design in this case will be...
questions.explain: The study needs closed questions (quantitative tallies) and open questions (qualitative reasons). It is not ethnographic, because there is no prolonged immersive observation.

questions.stem:
You are writing an essay on the credibility of an article on family communication. The article opens with this anecdote:

"Sunday evening in the Richardson home: parents scroll, teenagers text, the TV mutters to itself. They share a sofa but live on separate islands."

Guide yourself through PEEL to analyse this anecdote.

STEP 1: POINT

You must name the technique. What is it?

STEP 3: EXPLANATION

Explain how this technique works on the reader. What does the anecdote make you think or feel?
options: It places readers inside a familiar scene, so they recognize their own homes before the writer makes any argument. The embedded metaphor "separate island" (literal closeness but emotional distance) is especially powerful for a Caribbean audience where islands symbolize isolation.

questions.stem:
STEP 4: LINK

Connect this technique to the writer's purpose. Why does the writer use an anecdote and metaphor here?
options: The writer's purpose is to warn parents about device dependence. The anecdote and metaphor make the warning personal and relatable rather than abstract, so parents feel the problem is real and happening in their own homes. This makes them more likely to take the warning seriously.

questions.stem: In the listening section of Paper 1 (Items 1–7), how is the extract presented?
options: It is read aloud twice, and you may take notes during and between the readings.
It is read once only, and no notes are allowed.
It is played as a video recording.
It is printed in the question paper for you to read.

questions.stem:
Read each situation and drag it to the characteristic of language it best shows.

Which characteristic of language is shown?

The English say "dog", the Dutch say "hond" and Papiamentu speakers say "kachó".
questions.explain: Three different words for the same animal: nothing about the animal decides the word. That is arbitrariness.

questions.stem:
Which characteristic of language is shown?

There is no reason why the sounds in "tree" should mean a tall plant.
questions.explain: The link between sound and meaning is agreed by the community, not natural, so this is arbitrary.

questions.stem:
Which characteristic of language is shown?

"Cloud" now also means online storage.
questions.explain: The word has gained a new meaning over time: language is dynamic.

questions.stem:
Which characteristic of language is shown?

Words like "selfie" and "livestream" entered dictionaries recently.
questions.explain: New words appear as society changes. That is dynamism.

questions.stem:
Which characteristic of language is shown?

Uncle tells the story of the 1995 hurricane at the family lime.
questions.explain: He is talking about the past, something not here and now. That is displacement.

questions.stem:
Which characteristic of language is shown?

Two students plan what they will do after CAPE exams next year.
questions.explain: Talking about the future is displacement too.

questions.stem:
Which characteristic of language is shown?

A Bajan speaker says "I does go to school" but never "Does I go school to".
questions.explain: The habitual marker "does" has a fixed position in the sentence. Creoles are rule-governed, so this is systematic.

questions.stem:
Which characteristic of language is shown?

In Jamaican Creole the plural marker "dem" always follows the noun: "di gyal dem".
questions.explain: A fixed rule about word order shows that the language is systematic.

questions.stem:
Choose the characteristic or concept that each situation BEST illustrates.

Over a few generations, a contact language develops a full tense system and a much larger vocabulary.
questions.explain: The language has grown more complex over time: maturational.

questions.stem: Twins adopted at birth by a family in Aruba grow up speaking Papiamentu, not the language of their birth parents.
questions.explain: Language is not inherited; it is acquired from the community around the child: non-instinctive.

questions.stem: Students in a deaf school in Kingston debate in Jamaican Sign Language.
options: sign is a dialect of English
questions.explain: The syllabus defines language as spoken and sign. Sign languages have their own grammar.

questions.stem: "Every human community has language." Here "language" is used in the...
questions.explain: It refers to the human ability in general: the generic sense.

questions.stem: The word "ghost" now also means to stop replying to someone's messages.
questions.explain: A new meaning for an existing word is change: dynamic. Maturational is about growing complexity.

questions.stem:
At the bus stop on Bay Street, Mr. Lake nods to a young man he sees every morning. "Morning, youth. Hot today, eh?" The young man smiles. "Hot bad, Mr. Lake. Have a good one."

What is the MAIN function of the language in this exchange?

Answer each question. Think about what the language reveals.

A teenager uses Standard English in a scholarship interview and Guyanese Creolese on the basketball court. This mainly shows that language...
options: reflects and performs different parts of one identity
questions.explain: She is the same person showing different sides of herself to different audiences: language is linked to identity.

questions.stem: A teacher says, "Creole is just broken English." This statement reflects...
questions.explain: It is a belief about which variety is "proper", not a fact. Linguists recognise creoles as full languages with their own rules.

questions.stem: "Awful" once meant "full of awe" and now means "very bad". This shows...
options: a shift in accepted word meaning over time
questions.explain: The accepted meaning has changed as society used the word differently: language is dynamic and reflects social change.

questions.stem: A fishing village has many detailed words for types of nets, winds and currents. This suggests...
options: the community values and depends on fishing
questions.explain: Rich vocabulary in one area shows what matters to a society: language gives insight into the society that produces it.

questions.stem: Saying "speaky-spokey" about someone who uses very formal English reveals...
options: an attitude linked to class and belonging
questions.explain: The label hints that very formal speech can be seen as showing off or rejecting the group. It reveals social attitudes.

questions.stem:
You are interviewing for a summer job as a guest services assistant at a hotel in Grace Bay, Providenciales. Choose your words carefully: your register is being assessed as much as your answers.

The manager, Ms. Hodge, stands and offers her hand. "Good morning. Please, have a seat."

How do you respond?
options: "Good morning, Ms. Hodge. Thank you for seeing me."
Nod and sit down without speaking.

questions.stem: Ms. Hodge asks, "Why do you want to work in guest services?"
options: "Pursuant to my aspirations, I endeavour to facilitate tourism-related synergies."
"I enjoy meeting people and I am proud of our island. I would like to help visitors have a great experience while I build my customer-service skills."
"Ah need di money fi summer, dat's all."

questions.stem: At the end Ms. Hodge smiles: "Do you have any questions for me?"
options: "Yes, thank you. What would a typical day in this role involve?"

questions.stem: Andre from Guyana and Shanice from Barbados both read the same Standard English news script on air. Listeners can tell where each is from. What differs between them?
Which statement about standard and non-standard varieties is MOST accurate?
options: Standard English is spoken only in England.
A standard variety is the one codified and used for official purposes such as education, law and the media.
Non-standard varieties have no grammar rules.

questions.topic: Creole and Standard English: History and the Continuum
questions.stem:
Sort each sentence into the level of the continuum it best represents.

Basilect, mesolect or acrolect?

"Mi did a nyam mi food when im come."
questions.explain: "Mi", the pre-verbal markers "did a" and "nyam" make this broad creole: basilect.

questions.topic: Creole and Standard English: History and the Continuum
questions.stem:
Basilect, mesolect or acrolect?

"Unu ena go a di beach?"
questions.explain: "Unu" (you, plural) and "a di" are basilectal forms.

questions.topic: Creole and Standard English: History and the Continuum
questions.stem:
Basilect, mesolect or acrolect?

"Dem pickney a play ina di yard."
questions.explain: "Pickney", progressive "a" and "ina" mark this as basilect.

questions.topic: Creole and Standard English: History and the Continuum
questions.stem:
Basilect, mesolect or acrolect?

"She was going to the shop when it start rain."
questions.explain: Mostly standard, but "start rain" drops the past tense -ed and "to". A mix: mesolect.

questions.topic: Creole and Standard English: History and the Continuum
questions.stem:
Basilect, mesolect or acrolect?

"I not going to the fete tonight."
questions.explain: Standard words, but the copula "am" is missing. Mixed features: mesolect.

questions.topic: Creole and Standard English: History and the Continuum
questions.stem:
Basilect, mesolect or acrolect?

"Them children always playing in the yard."
questions.explain: "Them" as a determiner and the missing "are" show creole influence on mostly English vocabulary: mesolect.

questions.topic: Creole and Standard English: History and the Continuum
questions.stem:
Basilect, mesolect or acrolect?

"I was eating my food when he arrived."
questions.explain: Fully standard grammar: acrolect.

questions.topic: Creole and Standard English: History and the Continuum
questions.stem:
Basilect, mesolect or acrolect?

"Are you all going to the beach?"
questions.explain: Standard question form and copula: acrolect.

questions.topic: Creole and Standard English: History and the Continuum
questions.stem: Which of the following BEST explains why Haitian Creole is classified as a creole rather than a pidgin?
options: Most of its words come from French.
It is spoken in the Caribbean.
It is the first language of millions of speakers and has a complete grammar used for all purposes.

questions.topic: Creole and Standard English: History and the Continuum
questions.stem:
Six Paper 1-style questions from your class notes. Read every option before you choose.

Which of the following is a characteristic of language? It is...
questions.explain: Language is symbolic: words and signs stand for things and ideas. It is not instinctive (it is acquired from the community) or static (it is dynamic), and "directing" is a purpose, not a characteristic.

questions.topic: Creole and Standard English: History and the Continuum
questions.stem: All of the following are characteristics of language EXCEPT that it is...
questions.explain: Language is non-instinctive: it is acquired from the people around us, not inherited. Maturational, symbolic and dynamic are all characteristics named in the syllabus.

questions.topic: Creole and Standard English: History and the Continuum
questions.stem: Which indicate the functions of language in society? I. A medium for expression. II. A means to impart moral development. III. A mechanism for the growth of civilisation.
questions.explain: All three are roles language plays in society: it is a medium for expression, it passes on values and morals from one generation to the next (an ethical role), and it lets knowledge be recorded and built on, which supports the growth of civilisation (a social role). The syllabus asks you to analyse these social, political, ethical and psychological roles as well as the six functions.

questions.topic: Creole and Standard English: History and the Continuum
questions.stem: The national anthem is sung at school every Monday. Which function of language is shown?
questions.explain: The anthem is a song with a structured, literary form: the poetic (aesthetic) function. It gives no new information each week and is not private self-expression.

questions.topic: Creole and Standard English: History and the Continuum
questions.stem: Which of the following can be considered lingua francas?
options: English Creole, French Creole, Spanish Creole
questions.explain: The colonial source languages served as lingua francas. The creoles in the second option developed from them as native languages.

questions.topic: Creole and Standard English: History and the Continuum
questions.stem: All of the following account for the development of a creole EXCEPT...
options: recognition of creole as an official UN language
a concentration of pidgin speakers in one area
questions.explain: The UN's six official languages do not include a creole, and official recognition describes status, not how a creole develops.

questions.topic: The Wider Caribbean Language Situation: Origins, Diversity and Change
questions.stem: Languages such as Garifuna, Lokono, Patamona, Wapishana and Warao, all spoken in the Caribbean region, are MOST appropriately labelled

questions.topic: The Wider Caribbean Language Situation: Origins, Diversity and Change
questions.stem:
Sort each language into the correct type, using the syllabus distinction between Creole and non-Creole languages.

What type of language is it?

Papiamentu
options: Non-Creole: brought from outside the region
questions.explain: A native language that began in a contact situation: Creole.

questions.topic: The Wider Caribbean Language Situation: Origins, Diversity and Change
questions.stem:
What type of language is it?

Sranan Tongo
options: Non-Creole: brought from outside the region
questions.explain: An English-lexified creole of Suriname.

questions.topic: The Wider Caribbean Language Situation: Origins, Diversity and Change
questions.stem:
What type of language is it?

Haitian Creole
options: Non-Creole: brought from outside the region
questions.explain: A French-lexified creole.

questions.topic: The Wider Caribbean Language Situation: Origins, Diversity and Change
questions.stem:
What type of language is it?

Warao
options: Non-Creole: brought from outside the region
questions.explain: An indigenous language of Guyana and Venezuela, not a creole.

questions.topic: The Wider Caribbean Language Situation: Origins, Diversity and Change
questions.stem:
What type of language is it?

Garifuna
options: Non-Creole: brought from outside the region
questions.explain: An indigenous Arawakan language.

questions.topic: The Wider Caribbean Language Situation: Origins, Diversity and Change
questions.stem:
What type of language is it?

Q'eqchi' (Kekchi)
options: Non-Creole: brought from outside the region
questions.explain: A Mayan language spoken in Belize: indigenous.

questions.topic: The Wider Caribbean Language Situation: Origins, Diversity and Change
questions.stem:
What type of language is it?

Hindi / Bhojpuri
options: Non-Creole: brought from outside the region
questions.explain: Brought from India by indentured labourers: non-Creole.

questions.topic: The Wider Caribbean Language Situation: Origins, Diversity and Change
questions.stem:
What type of language is it?

Mandarin and Hakka
options: Non-Creole: brought from outside the region
questions.explain: Chinese varieties brought from Asia: non-Creole.

questions.topic: The Wider Caribbean Language Situation: Origins, Diversity and Change
questions.stem:
What type of language is it?

Dutch
options: Non-Creole: brought from outside the region
questions.explain: A European language brought by colonisers: non-Creole.

questions.topic: Features of Creole and Standard English
questions.stem:
Classify each underlined feature as phonological, grammatical or lexical.

Which level of language does the feature belong to?

"Mi tink so." (think)
questions.explain: "th" becomes "t": th-stopping, a sound feature.

questions.topic: Features of Creole and Standard English
questions.stem:
Which level of language does the feature belong to?

"Dat is di bes' one." (best)
questions.explain: The final "t" of the cluster "st" is dropped: consonant cluster reduction.

questions.topic: Features of Creole and Standard English
questions.stem:
Which level of language does the feature belong to?

"Di pickney dem outside." (the children)
questions.explain: "dem" after the noun marks plural: a grammatical feature.

questions.topic: Features of Creole and Standard English
questions.stem:
Which level of language does the feature belong to?

"He en come yet." (hasn't come)
questions.explain: "en" is a pre-verbal negative/past marker: grammatical.

questions.topic: Features of Creole and Standard English
questions.stem:
Which level of language does the feature belong to?

"Mi have three book." (three books)
questions.explain: No plural -s after a numeral is a grammatical feature.

questions.topic: Features of Creole and Standard English
questions.stem:
Which level of language does the feature belong to?

"Come nyam yuh food." (eat)
questions.explain: "nyam" is an African retention: a lexical feature.

questions.topic: Features of Creole and Standard English
questions.stem:
Which level of language does the feature belong to?

"Mi foot hurting from the knee." (leg)
questions.explain: "foot" meaning the whole leg is semantic shift: lexical.

questions.topic: Features of Creole and Standard English
questions.stem:
Which level of language does the feature belong to?

"Pass the roti." (Indian flatbread)
questions.explain: "roti" is a loanword from Indian languages: lexical.

questions.topic: Features of Creole and Standard English
questions.stem:
During the hurricane meeting at the community centre, the district officer explains the shelter plan in clear Standard English. Then he looks at the elderly residents in the front row and says, "Unu nuh fraid, we go come fi unu early."

What is the officer doing, and why?
options: Using diglossia, because Creole is the High variety.
Code-switching, to reassure the elderly residents and build trust.
Code-mixing, because he does not know enough Standard English.
Using a frozen register to show respect.

questions.stem:
Each statement shows an attitude. Sort it by the factor that best explains where the attitude came from.

Which factor produced this attitude?

"After a tourist couldn't understand me at work, I felt ashamed of my vernacular."
questions.explain: A specific event in the speaker's life produced the embarrassment: personal experience.

questions.stem:
Which factor produced this attitude?

"When I went to study in Holland, people loved my island English, and now I'm proud of it."
questions.explain: A particular experience abroad changed the speaker's feelings: personal experience.

questions.stem:
Which factor produced this attitude?

"In primary school we lost points for every Creole word in our compositions."
questions.explain: Schooling taught that Creole is "wrong": education.

questions.stem:
Which factor produced this attitude?

"Our English teacher said nobody would hire us if we spoke dialect."
questions.explain: The attitude was taught through school: education.

questions.stem:
Which factor produced this attitude?

"Grandma always slapped my hand if I answered her in dialect."
questions.explain: Family rules pass on the community's language ideology: socialisation.

questions.stem:
Which factor produced this attitude?

"In our church, everybody pray in proper English; dialect is for the street."
questions.explain: The community's beliefs shape the attitude: socialisation.

questions.stem:
Which factor produced this attitude?

"The colonial masters' language became the 'proper' one, and that idea never left."
questions.explain: The attitude is explained by the colonial past: history and society.

questions.stem:
Which factor produced this attitude?

"Because enslaved Africans' speech was mocked for centuries, Creole still carries stigma."
questions.explain: The sociohistorical development of Creole explains the stigma: history and society.

questions.stem:
When her son answered the phone with "Who dis?", Mrs. Carty snatched it from him. "How many times I must tell you? We don't talk like that in this house. People will think we have no class." Later she told her sister, "My own mother beat that dialect out of me, and I am doing the same for him."

Which answer BEST identifies Mrs. Carty's attitude and the factor that produced it?
options: A negative attitude, produced by education.
Indifference, produced by history and society.
Contempt for the vernacular, produced mainly by socialisation in her family.
Pride in Standard English, produced by personal experience.

questions.stem:
Choose the BEST answer for each short exam-style question.

"I don't care how people talk, once they get the job done." The best adjective for this attitude is...
questions.explain: The speaker places no value either way on the variety: indifference.

questions.stem: Which phrase would earn the MOST credit in an essay?
options: "She shows embarrassment, evident when she whispers, 'Sorry for my bad English.'"
questions.explain: It names a precise feeling AND supports it with an exact quotation.

questions.stem: A radio station plays Creole jingles but reads all news in Standard English. This may suggest that Creole is viewed as...
options: suitable for entertainment but not for serious information
questions.explain: The split in use reflects an evaluation of Creole's status in "serious" domains.

questions.stem: "Miss always told us Creole would hold us back in life." The factor is...
questions.explain: "Miss" is a teacher, so the attitude came through schooling: education.

questions.stem: In Sint Maarten, the language most residents use in daily life is...
questions.explain: Dutch is used for law and much government business, but English is the everyday language of most residents.

questions.stem:
Sort each situation by the role of language it MAINLY shows.

Social, political, ethical or psychological?

Friends in a group chat use island slang that outsiders cannot follow.
questions.explain: Language marks group membership and solidarity: social.

questions.stem:
Social, political, ethical or psychological?

A church choir greets each other with the same Papiamentu blessing every Sunday.
questions.explain: Shared language builds belonging: social.

questions.stem:
Social, political, ethical or psychological?

Parliament debates whether to make a creole an official language.
questions.explain: Language policy and status are political.

questions.stem:
Social, political, ethical or psychological?

Marchers chant slogans in Creole outside the Government Administration Building.
questions.explain: Language used to signal protest is political.

questions.stem:
Social, political, ethical or psychological?

A bank refuses to serve a customer because she cannot speak Standard English.
questions.explain: Unfair treatment because of language is an ethical issue.

questions.stem:
Social, political, ethical or psychological?

Hospital forms are printed only in a language many patients cannot read.
questions.explain: It denies people fair access to information: ethical.

questions.stem:
Social, political, ethical or psychological?

After being mocked for his accent, a boy refuses to read aloud in class.
questions.explain: Language affecting confidence and face: psychological.

questions.stem:
Social, political, ethical or psychological?

A student feels proud and confident performing a Creole poem.
questions.explain: Language shaping self-esteem: psychological.

questions.stem:
Marisol, who grew up in the Cayman Islands speaking Spanish at home and the island's English vernacular with friends, applies for a job as a hotel cleaner. The supervisor rejects her, saying, "We don't hire people who talk like that," although the job does not involve speaking to guests.

Which role of language is MOST clearly being breached by the supervisor?

Jaden, 18, is applying for a summer internship at a Bridgetown law firm. Help him make the right choices.

Jaden opens his email. Which address should he send the application from?
Which opening line suits the email?
options: "Dear Ms. Arrindell, I am writing to apply for the summer internship advertised on your website."

questions.stem: Jaden's friend says, "Just write it how you text, they'll understand." What should Jaden do?
options: Leave in abbreviations like "u" and "bc" to save time.
Proofread for full spelling and punctuation, keep a formal register, and sign off with his full name and phone number.

questions.topic: Communicative Behaviours and the Module 2 Essay
questions.stem:
Sort each description into the type of non-verbal behaviour it shows.

Which non-verbal code is this?

Auntie lets out a long steups when the bus driver passes her.
questions.explain: A vocal sound without words: paralanguage.

questions.topic: Communicative Behaviours and the Module 2 Essay
questions.stem:
Which non-verbal code is this?

The principal lowers his voice to almost a whisper before announcing the results.
questions.explain: Changing volume and tone is paralanguage.

questions.topic: Communicative Behaviours and the Module 2 Essay
questions.stem:
Which non-verbal code is this?

The student moves her chair away from the boy who teased her.
questions.explain: Using distance to send a message: proxemics.

questions.topic: Communicative Behaviours and the Module 2 Essay
questions.stem:
Which non-verbal code is this?

The minister arrives forty minutes late to the community meeting.
questions.explain: Lateness sends a message about priorities: chronemics.

questions.topic: Communicative Behaviours and the Module 2 Essay
questions.stem:
Which non-verbal code is this?

The coach squeezes the nervous player's shoulder.
questions.explain: Touch: haptics.

questions.topic: Communicative Behaviours and the Module 2 Essay
questions.stem:
Which non-verbal code is this?

Everyone wears red, white and blue on Constitution Day.
questions.explain: National colours carry a cultural message: chromatics.

questions.topic: Communicative Behaviours and the Module 2 Essay
questions.stem:
Which non-verbal code is this?

The family dresses in white for the thanksgiving service.
questions.explain: The colour white conveys meaning (purity, celebration or mourning, depending on context): chromatics.

questions.topic: Communicative Behaviours and the Module 2 Essay
questions.stem:
You are a CAPE student analysing an extract for Paper 2. Choose the best interpretation at each step. Remember: ask WHO and WHY.

Before the final exam, Ms. Daniel stands at the door. As Rhea passes, Ms. Daniel squeezes her hand and holds her gaze for a moment.

What does the hand squeeze most likely communicate here?
options: Encouragement and reassurance before a stressful exam.

questions.topic: Communicative Behaviours and the Module 2 Essay
questions.stem:
Later, in the staff room, Mr. Gumbs arrives twenty minutes late to the department meeting, sits at the back, and scrolls on his phone. The head of department glances at the clock and folds her arms.

Which interpretation is best supported?
options: He is clearly very busy and committed to his work.
His chronemics, proxemics and phone use suggest disengagement; her glance at the clock and folded arms suggest disapproval.

questions.topic: Communicative Behaviours and the Module 2 Essay
questions.stem: How would you write this in your essay?
options: "Mr. Gumbs's late arrival (chronemics) and choice to sit at the back (proxemics) suggest indifference, which the head of department meets with visible disapproval, shown by her glance at the clock and folded arms."
"There is a lot of body language in the staff room."

questions.topic: Communicative Behaviours and the Module 2 Essay
questions.stem:
Now sort across the full set of non-verbal codes, including oculesics (eye behaviour) and artefacts (objects and appearance).

Which non-verbal code is MAINLY at work?

The prefect folds her arms and shakes her head as the boys push into the lunch line.
questions.explain: Posture and head movement: kinesics (body language).

questions.topic: Communicative Behaviours and the Module 2 Essay
questions.stem:
Which non-verbal code is MAINLY at work?

Granny gives the child a long cut-eye across the church pew.
questions.explain: A look that carries scorn: oculesics, the study of eye behaviour.

questions.topic: Communicative Behaviours and the Module 2 Essay
questions.stem:
Which non-verbal code is MAINLY at work?

The interviewee holds steady eye contact with each panel member as she answers.
questions.explain: Eye contact signals confidence and honesty here: oculesics.

questions.topic: Communicative Behaviours and the Module 2 Essay
questions.stem:
Which non-verbal code is MAINLY at work?

The new student sits at the far end of the bench, away from everyone.
questions.explain: Use of distance and space: proxemics.

questions.topic: Communicative Behaviours and the Module 2 Essay
questions.stem:
Which non-verbal code is MAINLY at work?

The tour guide slows down and lowers his pitch to tell the ghost story of the old fort.
questions.explain: Pace and pitch of the voice: paralanguage (vocalics).

questions.topic: Communicative Behaviours and the Module 2 Essay
questions.stem:
Which non-verbal code is MAINLY at work?

Teammates exchange fist bumps after the winning goal.
questions.explain: Touch: haptics.

questions.topic: Communicative Behaviours and the Module 2 Essay
questions.stem:
Which non-verbal code is MAINLY at work?

The applicant arrives fifteen minutes early for the interview.
questions.explain: Use of time sends a message of respect: chronemics.

questions.topic: Communicative Behaviours and the Module 2 Essay
questions.stem:
Which non-verbal code is MAINLY at work?

The lawyer wears a dark suit, a gold watch and carries a leather briefcase into court.
questions.explain: Clothing and objects communicate status and professionalism: artefacts.

questions.topic: Communicative Behaviours and the Module 2 Essay
questions.stem:
Which non-verbal code is MAINLY at work?

The receptionist's desk displays her diplomas and a small Belizean flag.
questions.explain: Objects arranged in a space communicate identity and credibility: artefacts.

questions.topic: Communicative Behaviours and the Module 2 Essay
questions.stem: The question asks you to discuss the language varieties, attitudes and communicative behaviours in an extract. Which thesis statement is BEST?
options: "This essay will discuss the attitudes in the extract."
"This essay will talk about language in the extract."
"Creole is a beautiful language that everyone should be proud of."
"This essay will examine the shift between Creole and Standard English, the contrasting attitudes of embarrassment and pride, and the gestures and paralanguage that reveal them."

questions.stem:
During a parent-teacher meeting, Mr. Hodge explains Kayla's grades. As he speaks, he notices her mother frowning and folding her arms, so he slows down and adds, "But she has improved a lot since October." The mother relaxes and nods while asking a question.

Which model of communication BEST describes this exchange?

A tourism office in Saint Lucia ran a month-long radio and Instagram campaign urging cruise visitors to shop at local craft markets. The director now wants to know whether the campaign changed visitors' behaviour.

Which model would be MOST useful for analysing this campaign, and why?
options: The interactive model, because Instagram users take turns posting.
Lasswell's model, because its final question, "with what effect?", focuses on the campaign's impact on its audience.
The transactional model, because the director and visitors talk face to face.
Berlo's model, because it shows that channels are the five senses.

questions.stem:
A station, Harbour FM, broadcasts a hurricane watch for Anguilla. Sort each detail: is it part of the content (what is said) or the context (where, when, to whom, why)?

Content or context?

"A hurricane watch is now in effect for Anguilla."
questions.explain: These are the actual words of the message, so this is content.

questions.stem:
Content or context?

"Secure loose objects in your yard and fill water containers."
questions.explain: Instructions spoken in the broadcast are part of what is said: content.

questions.stem:
Content or context?

"Shelters will open at noon tomorrow."
questions.explain: Another piece of information in the message itself: content.

questions.stem:
Content or context?

It is broadcast at 6 a.m., while many people are getting ready for work.
questions.explain: This tells us WHEN the message is sent, so it is context.

questions.stem:
Content or context?

Listeners include fishermen, hotel workers and elderly residents.
questions.explain: This tells us TO WHOM the message is sent, so it is context.

questions.stem:
Content or context?

The aim is to help people prepare before the winds arrive.
questions.explain: This is WHY the message is sent, its purpose, which is part of the context.

questions.stem:
Content or context?

It is the peak of hurricane season, two weeks after another storm.
questions.explain: The wider situation and timing shape how people hear the message: context.

questions.stem:
Content or context?

The message is read from the station's studio in The Valley.
questions.explain: This is WHERE the message comes from: context.

questions.stem:
Each sentence describes one element of the communication process. Identify it.

A loud generator outside the classroom drowns out the teacher's voice.
questions.explain: The generator interferes with the message, so it is physical noise.

questions.stem: A student raises her hand and says, "Sir, can you repeat that?"
questions.explain: The student is responding to the message, which is feedback. Asking for repetition is very useful feedback because it shows the message was not fully received.

questions.stem: The minister chooses simple words and a local example for his press release.
questions.explain: Choosing words and examples is encoding: turning ideas into symbols.

questions.stem: Listeners work out that "batten down" means they must secure their homes.
questions.explain: Interpreting the meaning of words is decoding.

questions.stem: The message is posted as a flyer on the supermarket notice board.
questions.explain: The flyer is the form or vehicle carrying the message, the medium.

questions.topic: Audience, Context and Forms of Communication
questions.stem:
The Sandy Ground Seniors' Club wants to tell its members, most of them over 70 and many of whom left school early, about a change in the date of its monthly lunch. Members live in several districts; a few do not own mobile phones, but almost all attend Sunday service.

Based on the audience profile, which medium and channel would be MOST effective?
options: A detailed email newsletter explaining the reasons for the change.
A spoken announcement after Sunday service, backed up by a large-print flyer and phone calls to those who were absent.
An Instagram story with a countdown sticker.
A press release to the national newspaper.

questions.topic: Audience, Context and Forms of Communication
questions.stem:
At Flamboyant Heights College in Barbados, decide the direction or network of each message.

The principal sends a circular to all teachers about new coursework deadlines.
questions.explain: From the top of the hierarchy to staff below: downward.

questions.topic: Audience, Context and Forms of Communication
questions.stem: A form teacher writes to the vice-principal requesting more desks for her class.
questions.explain: A request from a subordinate to a superior: upward.

questions.topic: Audience, Context and Forms of Communication
questions.stem: The heads of Science and Mathematics meet to plan a STEM week together.
questions.explain: Same level, different departments: horizontal (lateral).

questions.topic: Audience, Context and Forms of Communication
questions.stem: In the staff room, someone whispers that the principal may be transferred.
questions.explain: Unofficial talk that is not confirmed is the grapevine.

questions.topic: Audience, Context and Forms of Communication
questions.stem: The Student Council president submits a report on canteen complaints to the principal.
questions.explain: Students reporting to the principal is upward communication.

questions.topic: Audience, Context and Forms of Communication
questions.stem:
At the Harbour View Hotel in Montego Bay, sort each message by the direction or network it travels through.

Which direction of organisational communication?

The general manager emails all supervisors the new hurricane-season procedures.
questions.explain: From the top of the hierarchy to those below: downward.

questions.topic: Audience, Context and Forms of Communication
questions.stem:
Which direction of organisational communication?

A housekeeper submits a written suggestion to her supervisor about safer cleaning chemicals.
questions.explain: From a subordinate to a superior: upward.

questions.topic: Audience, Context and Forms of Communication
questions.stem:
Which direction of organisational communication?

The front-desk supervisor and the restaurant supervisor agree on breakfast times for a tour group.
questions.explain: Two people at the same level coordinating: horizontal.

questions.topic: Audience, Context and Forms of Communication
questions.stem:
Which direction of organisational communication?

The head of accounts phones a junior chef directly to query a missing supplier invoice.
questions.explain: Different department AND different level, bypassing the chef's own manager: diagonal (cross-channel).

questions.topic: Audience, Context and Forms of Communication
questions.stem:
Which direction of organisational communication?

The marketing manager messages a front-desk clerk to collect guests' feedback cards for a report.
questions.explain: A manager in one department contacting a junior worker in another: diagonal.

questions.topic: Audience, Context and Forms of Communication
questions.stem:
Which direction of organisational communication?

Staff whisper in the canteen that the hotel is about to be sold.
questions.explain: Unofficial, unconfirmed talk: the grapevine.

questions.topic: Barriers (Noise) and How to Repair Them
questions.stem:
A youth council in Antigua is holding a public meeting about a new skate park. Things keep going wrong. Sort each problem into the correct type of barrier.

What type of barrier is each problem?

The meeting is outdoors and a jet landing at the airport drowns out the speaker.
questions.explain: Noise from the environment is a physical barrier.

questions.topic: Barriers (Noise) and How to Repair Them
questions.stem:
What type of barrier is each problem?

An elderly resident with a hearing impairment cannot follow the discussion.
questions.explain: A condition of the body is a physiological barrier.

questions.topic: Barriers (Noise) and How to Repair Them
questions.stem:
What type of barrier is each problem?

One parent is so angry about noise from skaters that he refuses to listen to the plan.
questions.explain: Strong emotion and a closed mind are psychological barriers.

questions.topic: Barriers (Noise) and How to Repair Them
questions.stem:
What type of barrier is each problem?

The engineer keeps saying "load-bearing substrate" and "ingress points".
questions.explain: Technical jargon is a semantic barrier.

questions.topic: Barriers (Noise) and How to Repair Them
questions.stem:
What type of barrier is each problem?

Several Spanish-speaking residents do not understand the English presentation.
questions.explain: A language difference is a semantic (linguistic) barrier. You could also discuss it as cultural, but the core problem is language.

questions.topic: Barriers (Noise) and How to Repair Them
questions.stem:
What type of barrier is each problem?

The projector will not connect to the laptop, so nobody sees the design.
questions.explain: Equipment failure is a technological barrier.

questions.topic: Barriers (Noise) and How to Repair Them
questions.stem:
What type of barrier is each problem?

Teenagers stop listening because they assume the adults are against them.
questions.explain: Assumptions and prejudice are psychological barriers.

questions.topic: Barriers (Noise) and How to Repair Them
questions.stem:
What type of barrier is each problem?

The livestream for people at home keeps freezing.
questions.explain: Poor connectivity is a technological barrier.

questions.topic: Barriers (Noise) and How to Repair Them
questions.stem:
The Ministry of Public Health wants to warn residents in a densely populated district about a dengue outbreak. Many residents are recent migrants who speak Spanish or Haitian Creole, and some have low literacy. A previous English-language newspaper notice had little effect.

Which strategy would MOST effectively overcome the main barriers in this situation?
options: Print a longer, more detailed notice in the English newspaper.
Ask school principals to email parents in formal English.
Post a detailed video on the Ministry's website.
Send community health workers door-to-door with picture-based flyers and messages in Spanish and Haitian Creole.

questions.topic: Barriers (Noise) and How to Repair Them
questions.stem: Two days later, three night staff say they never saw the email: they do not have work email on their phones. Another mix-up happens. What now?
options: Hold a meeting at shift changeover and go through the procedure in person.
Blame the night staff for not checking email.

questions.topic: Barriers (Noise) and How to Repair Them
questions.stem:
At the meeting, the day supervisor folds his arms and says, "I posted it. Not my fault if they can't read a notice." A night clerk rolls her eyes. The tension is obvious.

How do you respond?
options: Acknowledge both sides calmly, focus on the system rather than blame, and ask, "How can we make sure every shift gets every update?"
Tell the supervisor in front of everyone that he is to blame.

questions.topic: Barriers (Noise) and How to Repair Them
questions.stem: Staff suggest a few ideas. Which plan do you adopt?
options: Continue with the notice board but make the font bigger.
A short written handover log signed by each shift, a weekly 10-minute briefing, and urgent updates read aloud at changeover and confirmed by signature.

questions.stem:
A Grenadian tour company is moving all staff communication from printed notices and phone calls to an online messaging app. Sort each point.

Is each point an advantage or a disadvantage of the new medium?

Tour guides at different beaches get updates instantly.
questions.explain: Speed and reach across locations is a key advantage of new media.

questions.stem:
Is each point an advantage or a disadvantage of the new medium?

Older drivers struggle to use the app.
questions.explain: Lack of skills is part of the digital divide, and it is also an age barrier.

questions.stem:
Is each point an advantage or a disadvantage of the new medium?

Messages are stored, so instructions can be checked later.
questions.explain: A searchable record is an advantage.

questions.stem:
Is each point an advantage or a disadvantage of the new medium?

A joke in the chat is taken as an insult because there is no tone of voice.
questions.explain: Loss of non-verbal cues causes misunderstanding in text-based media.

questions.stem:
Is each point an advantage or a disadvantage of the new medium?

Photos of damaged vehicles can be sent to the mechanic immediately.
questions.explain: Multimedia makes the message clearer than words alone.

questions.stem:
Is each point an advantage or a disadvantage of the new medium?

After a storm, the app is useless because mobile networks are down.
questions.explain: Dependence on infrastructure is a serious disadvantage in the Caribbean. This is why old media such as battery radio remain important.

questions.stem:
Is each point an advantage or a disadvantage of the new medium?

Staff receive messages at 2 a.m. and feel they must reply.
questions.explain: Blurred work-life boundaries can cause stress.

questions.stem:
Two days before a local election, a video spreads on WhatsApp. It appears to show a well-known candidate saying she will close the Grand Anse health clinic. The candidate never said this; her face and voice were digitally inserted into someone else's recording.

Which term BEST describes this video?

You lead the Clean Coast Youth Group in Grenada. Your campaign wants the government to install more bins at Gouyave. A member brings you a shocking video. Make the ethical decisions.

The video shows a beach buried in rubbish. It is getting thousands of views. Your member admits, "It's actually from another country, but nobody will know. If we post it as Gouyave, people will finally care."

What do you do?
options: Refuse to post it as Gouyave, and instead plan to collect real evidence from the beach.
Post it with the caption "Gouyave this morning! Shameful!"
Post it without a caption and let people assume.

questions.stem:
On Saturday your team photographs real litter at Gouyave and counts the bottles collected in one hour. The photos are less dramatic than the viral video. A member says, "These won't go viral. Let's at least add a few more bottles to the pile before we take the picture."

What do you say?
options: "No. We use what we found. Let's make it powerful with honest storytelling and good timing instead."
"Fine, a few extra bottles won't hurt anyone."

questions.stem: How will you present your honest campaign?
options: Post the real photos with no explanation at midnight on a Tuesday.

Post the real photos with your one-hour bottle count, a short video of a young turtle tangled in plastic you actually freed, and release it the week before the cruise season opens, tagging the relevant ministry.

questions.stem:
These lines come from a student campaign encouraging residents to donate blood at the Kingstown Blood Drive. Sort each line by its MAIN appeal.

Which appeal does each line mainly use?

"One donation takes about ten minutes and can help more than one patient."
questions.explain: A practical, reasoned benefit: logos.

questions.stem:
Which appeal does each line mainly use?

"Donated blood cannot be manufactured; hospitals depend entirely on volunteers."
questions.explain: A logical fact that explains why donors are needed: logos.

questions.stem:
Which appeal does each line mainly use?

"As a nurse at the hospital for fifteen years, I see every day what your donation does."
questions.explain: The speaker's experience and role build credibility: ethos.

questions.stem:
Which appeal does each line mainly use?

"Endorsed by the island's medical association."
questions.explain: An authoritative source lends credibility: ethos.

questions.stem:
Which appeal does each line mainly use?

"Imagine a little boy waiting for blood that nobody gave."
questions.explain: An emotional image to stir compassion: pathos.

questions.stem:
Which appeal does each line mainly use?

"Be the hero your neighbour needs."
questions.explain: Pride and belonging: pathos.

questions.stem:
Which appeal does each line mainly use?

"Hurricane season is coming, and the blood bank must be full before the storms."
questions.explain: Linking the message to the right moment: kairos.

questions.stem:
Which appeal does each line mainly use?

"The drive ends this Saturday. Don't miss your chance."
questions.explain: A deadline creates urgency: kairos.

questions.stem:
"It's Carnival time, St. Kitts! Feel the soca in your soul at Village Fete this Saturday night! Early-bird tickets are half price until Wednesday, and free shuttle buses run all night, so nobody has to drink and drive."

Which combination of appeals does this radio advert MAINLY use?

Sort each example by the MAIN function the non-verbal or paralinguistic cue performs.

What is the cue doing?

The bus driver waves the passenger on without a word.
questions.explain: The wave replaces the words "get on": substituting.

questions.stem:
What is the cue doing?

The principal says "Absolutely not" and shakes her head firmly.
questions.explain: The head shake repeats and strengthens the words: reinforcing.

questions.stem:
What is the cue doing?

The chairperson raises her hand and looks at the next speaker to give him the floor.
questions.explain: The cues control turn-taking: regulating.

questions.stem:
What is the cue doing?

A student says "I'm really excited about this project" in a bored monotone.
questions.explain: The voice contradicts the words.

questions.stem:
What is the cue doing?

A job applicant chooses a neat suit and a firm handshake to appear professional.
questions.explain: Dress and touch are chosen to shape how others see him: managing impression.

questions.stem:
What is the cue doing?

A grandmother holds her grandson's hand throughout the hospital visit.
questions.explain: Touch expresses closeness and trust: establishing relationship.

questions.stem:
What is the cue doing?

A speaker pauses and lowers her voice just before announcing the winner.
questions.explain: The pause signals that something important is coming, guiding how the message is received: regulating.

questions.stem:
At Linstead Community Centre, Mr. Gumbs's neighbour has just lost her home in a fire. She talks for a long time about what happened. Mr. Gumbs says little, nods, keeps gentle eye contact and occasionally says, "That must have been terrifying."

Which type of listening is Mr. Gumbs MAINLY using?

questions.topic: The Writing Process, Meetings and Digital Communication
questions.stem:
Sort each form of communication.

Is this mainly a form of speaking or of writing?

A toast at a wedding reception
questions.explain: A toast is delivered aloud.

questions.topic: The Writing Process, Meetings and Digital Communication
questions.stem:
Is this mainly a form of speaking or of writing?

A memorandum to all staff
questions.explain: A memo is a written document.

questions.topic: The Writing Process, Meetings and Digital Communication
questions.stem:
Is this mainly a form of speaking or of writing?

A eulogy at a funeral
questions.explain: A eulogy is spoken.

questions.topic: The Writing Process, Meetings and Digital Communication
questions.stem:
Is this mainly a form of speaking or of writing?

A meeting agenda
questions.explain: An agenda is written and circulated.

questions.topic: The Writing Process, Meetings and Digital Communication
questions.stem:
Is this mainly a form of speaking or of writing?

A pamphlet on dengue prevention
questions.explain: A pamphlet is a written form.

questions.topic: The Writing Process, Meetings and Digital Communication
questions.stem:
Is this mainly a form of speaking or of writing?

A valedictory address at graduation
questions.explain: A valedictory address is a speech.

questions.topic: The Writing Process, Meetings and Digital Communication
questions.stem:
Is this mainly a form of speaking or of writing?

A press conference after a storm
questions.explain: A press conference is spoken and interactive.

questions.topic: The Writing Process, Meetings and Digital Communication
questions.stem:
Is this mainly a form of speaking or of writing?

A text message to a classmate
questions.explain: A text message is written, even if informal.

questions.topic: The Writing Process, Meetings and Digital Communication
questions.stem: The secretary of the Carrot Bay Residents' Association needs a document, sent to members a week ahead, that lists in order: apologies, confirmation of last meeting's minutes, matters arising, a report on street lighting, and any other business. Which document is this?

questions.topic: The Writing Process, Meetings and Digital Communication
questions.stem:
Paper 1-style questions from your class notes. Read every option before you choose.

Two means of WRITING that could capture students' interest in a campaign about vaping are...
questions.explain: Drama, a poetry recital and a speech are spoken or performed, not written. Pamphlets and posters are both written forms.

questions.topic: The Writing Process, Meetings and Digital Communication
questions.stem: A speaker's teenage audience becomes disengaged. Which of the following is NOT a feature of the speaker's voice that could explain this?
questions.explain: Pitch, monotone and volume are vocal features of delivery. Dress may affect how the audience receives the speaker, but it is not a feature of the voice.

questions.topic: The Writing Process, Meetings and Digital Communication
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT essential for a good written report?
questions.explain: Bulleted points can be useful but are not a necessity. Paragraphing, sentence structure and transitions are essential.

questions.topic: The Writing Process, Meetings and Digital Communication
questions.stem: A COVID-19 advertisement aimed at young people is MOST likely to be remembered because of its...
questions.explain: Music is the feature most likely to capture and hold young people's attention and stay in their memory.

questions.topic: The Writing Process, Meetings and Digital Communication
questions.stem: In a "Stay at Home" advertisement, the words "stay at home" are repeated throughout as a punchline. The dominant language technique is...
questions.explain: The phrase is repeated again and again: repetition.

questions.topic: The Writing Process, Meetings and Digital Communication
questions.stem: The Prime Minister addresses the nation on television. The context of communication is...
questions.explain: A leader speaking to the whole nation is a public context.

questions.topic: The Writing Process, Meetings and Digital Communication
questions.stem: Two pre-writing tasks for an essay on airborne diseases are...
questions.explain: Clustering is a pre-writing activity; editing, reviewing and rewriting belong to later stages.

questions.topic: The Writing Process, Meetings and Digital Communication
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a benefit of essay writing?
questions.explain: An essay is one-way communication: the reader cannot respond while reading.

questions.topic: The Writing Process, Meetings and Digital Communication
questions.stem: Two audiovisual aids suitable for a nursery class of three- and four-year-olds are...
questions.explain: Audiovisual means seen AND heard. Radio is audio only; posters, charts, books and crayons are visual only.

questions.topic: The Writing Process, Meetings and Digital Communication
questions.stem:
You are secretary of your school's Environment Club. Members are spread across the island during the holidays, and you must organise a planning meeting for a beach clean-up.

Twelve members need to discuss and agree on the clean-up plan this week, but they live in different districts. Which channel do you choose for the meeting?
options: A long voice note in the group chat explaining the plan.
A scheduled video conference, with the notice and agenda emailed three days ahead.

questions.topic: The Writing Process, Meetings and Digital Communication
questions.stem: During the call, one member keeps interrupting with his microphone on while music plays loudly in the background. What do you do as secretary, with the chair's agreement?
options: Post a message in capital letters telling him to SHUT UP.
Politely remind everyone to mute when not speaking and to use "raise hand" to take turns.

questions.topic: The Writing Process, Meetings and Digital Communication
questions.stem: After the meeting, a member suggests posting a screenshot of everyone's faces on the club's public page. What do you advise?
options: Ask for everyone's permission first, and post a group photo only if all agree.
Post it immediately; it's good publicity.

questions.topic: Letters, Proposals, Campaigns and the Module 3 Response
questions.stem:
Dear Sir/Madam,
Re: Littering at the Hastings boardwalk
I'm writing as secretary of the Clean Coast Youth Group cause the boardwalk is real nasty after weekends. We'd like you to put more bins.
Yours sincerely,
Jalen

Which revision would MOST improve this letter's register and conventions?
options: Remove the subject line because it is unnecessary.
Add more detail about how dirty the beach is, using stronger words.
Remove contractions and slang, use formal Standard English, change the close to "Yours faithfully", and add a full name and role.
Change "Dear Sir/Madam" to "Hi there" to sound friendlier.

questions.topic: Letters, Proposals, Campaigns and the Module 3 Response
questions.stem:
Examiners often change one or two words. For each task, decide what the answer must contain.

"Explain TWO message points related to logos OR pathos appeals." What must you give?
options: One logos point and one ethos point
Two message points, each explained in terms of logos or pathos
A list of all four appeals
questions.explain: Exactly two message points, each linked to logos or pathos and explained. Ethos and kairos are not asked for here.

questions.topic: Letters, Proposals, Campaigns and the Module 3 Response
questions.stem: "Justify ONE language register and ONE dialectal variety." Which pair answers this?
questions.explain: A register (formal, consultative, casual) and a dialectal variety (Standard English, a Creole/vernacular). PowerPoint is a technology; pathos is an appeal.

questions.topic: Letters, Proposals, Campaigns and the Module 3 Response
questions.stem: "Justify ONE digital media technology." Which answer fits best?
options: A Canva slideshow on a smart TV, because it is attractive and easy to update
questions.explain: Name one specific digital tool and justify it. A transistor radio is not digital, and "technology" is too vague.

questions.topic: Letters, Proposals, Campaigns and the Module 3 Response
questions.stem: Your answer is 380 words. What should you do?
options: Leave it; more words earn more marks
Cut it to 300 or fewer by removing repetition and padding
questions.explain: Module 3 responses are capped at 300 words. Cut repetition and padding, but keep a short conclusion.

questions.topic: Letters, Proposals, Campaigns and the Module 3 Response
questions.stem:
You chair the Coralstone College Road Safety Committee. You have been asked to plan a campaign to reduce speeding among young drivers in Grenada. Make the planning decisions.

Your committee is eager to start making posters immediately. What do you do first?
options: Design a poster with lots of statistics and start printing.
Profile the audience: drivers aged 17 to 25, their schooling, where they drive, and which media they use.

questions.topic: Letters, Proposals, Campaigns and the Module 3 Response
questions.stem: Your profile shows most young drivers spend hours on Instagram and TikTok, listen to the radio in the car, and see themselves as skilled drivers. Which message and appeals will you use?
options: "Arrive alive: the road is not a racetrack." A short real story from a young crash survivor (pathos), with the simple fact that higher speed means longer stopping distance (logos), launched before Carnival weekend (kairos).
"Speeding is illegal and you will be punished."

questions.topic: Letters, Proposals, Campaigns and the Module 3 Response
questions.stem: Which media and channels, and which barrier plan?
options: A press release to the newspaper only.

Short videos on Instagram and TikTok, radio spots during evening drive time, and talks in fifth-form classes; repair barriers by using the young people's own language style (within good taste), adding captions for viewers who watch without sound, and posting in English and Spanish.

questions.stem:
Shania is packing for Paper 032 (2026 topic: natural disasters). Sort each item.

Items in Shania's bag

One double-sided A4 sheet with 9 points on the exam topic
questions.explain: One card, correct size, under 10 points, related to the topic. That is exactly what is permitted.

questions.stem:
Items in Shania's bag

A second notes sheet "just in case"
questions.explain: Only a single notes sheet is allowed, even if she never looks at it.

questions.stem:
Items in Shania's bag

A notes sheet with 15 points in tiny writing
questions.explain: No more than 10 points. Fifteen breaks the rule, and tiny writing is useless under pressure anyway.

questions.stem:
Items in Shania's bag

A printed government hurricane guide
questions.explain: Nothing else is permitted. The key facts from the guide belong on the card as short points.

questions.stem:
Items in Shania's bag

A notes sheet with 10 short points on natural disasters
questions.explain: Ten points is the maximum, and it is allowed if the points relate to her topic.

questions.stem:
Items in Shania's bag

Her phone, switched off, "for the figures"
questions.explain: No phones. If a figure matters, it goes on the card.

questions.stem:
A 2026-style stimulus: a newspaper PSA from a Disaster Management Office telling homeowners to register for a free roof inspection before hurricane season. One question reads: "Explain TWO reasons why the public service announcement uses the dialectal variety and the language register which it does."

Which Module and question does this belong to?
options: It is not linked to a Module

questions.stem:
Quick-fire questions on the paper's format.

How long is Paper 032 according to the regulations?
questions.explain: The regulations give 2 hours 15 minutes.

questions.stem: How much does it contribute to the final assessment?
questions.explain: 60 marks, contributing 20 per cent.

questions.stem: How many marks is Section B worth?
questions.explain: Section B: piece (25) + justification (15) = 40.

questions.stem: What length is the Section B piece in the specimen?
questions.explain: Between 200 and 250 words.

questions.stem: The intended audience for 2027 is...
questions.explain: 2027: non-communicable diseases in children, for parents.

questions.topic: Section A, Question 1: Receiving Information, Media and Sources
questions.stem:
2027-style stimulus: A Ministry of Health PSA in a weekend newspaper tells parents that free blood-sugar screening for children aged 8–12 is available, but appointments must be booked through a new online portal.

Which response would earn the FULL 2 marks for ONE challenge parents in a low-income district are likely to face in receiving this information?
options: "The newspaper is a good way to communicate with parents."
"Some parents may not buy the weekend newspaper because of its cost, so they would never see the notice about free screening for their children."

questions.topic: Section A, Question 1: Receiving Information, Media and Sources
questions.stem:
The question asks: "Justify TWO appropriate traditional media, other than the printed medium, for informing elderly homeowners in a hillside village about free roof inspections." Sort each medium.

Media options

Radio
questions.explain: Traditional, not print, and very well suited to older listeners across the island.

questions.topic: Section A, Question 1: Receiving Information, Media and Sources
questions.stem:
Media options

A mobile loudspeaker van driving through the village
questions.explain: Traditional, oral, and reaches people where they live.

questions.topic: Section A, Question 1: Receiving Information, Media and Sources
questions.stem:
Media options

Word of mouth through church and village leaders
questions.explain: Traditional and suited to people who prefer orature, though best backed up by another medium.

questions.topic: Section A, Question 1: Receiving Information, Media and Sources
questions.stem:
Media options

A newspaper advertisement
questions.explain: The question says other than the printed medium. A newspaper is print.

questions.topic: Section A, Question 1: Receiving Information, Media and Sources
questions.stem:
Media options

An Instagram story
questions.explain: Social media is digital, not traditional, and many elderly homeowners may not use it.

questions.topic: Section A, Question 1: Receiving Information, Media and Sources
questions.stem:
Media options

A flyer in the post office
questions.explain: A flyer is printed, so it is excluded.

questions.topic: Section A, Question 1: Receiving Information, Media and Sources
questions.stem:
Media options

Television
questions.explain: Traditional, not print, with visual and aural appeal for demonstrating repairs.

questions.topic: Section A, Question 2: Variety, Register, Message Points and Slogans
questions.stem:
2027-style stimulus: a Ministry of Health PSA reads, "Parents and guardians are advised that free blood-glucose screening for children aged 8–12 will be available at all community clinics from 2 March. Appointments must be scheduled in advance."

Which answer to Q2(a) would earn the FULL 4 marks?
options: "It uses Creole so that parents feel at home."
"The language is good and easy to understand."
"It uses Standard English and a formal register."

"It uses Standard English because that is the official variety used by government, giving the notice authority. It uses a formal register because a ministry is addressing parents about a serious health matter, and a casual tone would make it seem less important."

questions.topic: Section A, Question 2: Variety, Register, Message Points and Slogans
questions.stem:
For each 2026 message aimed at homeowners, choose the BEST description.

"Homeowners are reminded that hurricane shutters must be installed before an official warning is issued."
questions.explain: Passive voice, official vocabulary and no contractions: Standard English in a formal register.

questions.topic: Section A, Question 2: Variety, Register, Message Points and Slogans
questions.stem: "Ay, neighbour! Yuh roof tie down good? Storm season reach!"
questions.explain: "Yuh", "tie down good" and "reach" are Creole features, and the greeting is casual.

questions.topic: Section A, Question 2: Variety, Register, Message Points and Slogans
questions.stem: "Hey homeowners! Got your hurricane kit ready? Here are five quick checks."
questions.explain: The grammar is Standard English, but the tone is chatty and friendly: informal register.

questions.topic: Section A, Question 2: Variety, Register, Message Points and Slogans
questions.stem: Why would a ministry use the FIRST message's style?
options: Creole is not allowed on paper
It wants to sound like a friend
It is official communication on a serious matter
questions.explain: Government communication is official and serious, so it uses Standard English in a formal register.

questions.topic: Section B: The Reflective or Expository Piece
questions.stem:
Sort each opening line (2026 or 2027 topic) by form.

Opening lines

"I still remember the silence after the wind stopped, and the morning light pouring through the hole where our kitchen roof had been."
questions.explain: First person, memory and feeling: reflective.

questions.topic: Section B: The Reflective or Expository Piece
questions.stem:
Opening lines

"Every homeowner in Jamaica can take five simple, low-cost steps to protect their property before hurricane season."
questions.explain: An informing thesis aimed at readers: expository.

questions.topic: Section B: The Reflective or Expository Piece
questions.stem:
Opening lines

"Non-communicable diseases in children are rising across the Caribbean, but parents hold the most powerful tools to reverse the trend."
questions.explain: States a main point and promises explanation: expository essay.

questions.topic: Section B: The Reflective or Expository Piece
questions.stem:
Opening lines

"The day the nurse said 'pre-diabetic', I looked at the juice box in my son's hand and felt my stomach drop."
questions.explain: A personal moment and a feeling: reflective.

questions.topic: Section B: The Reflective or Expository Piece
questions.stem:
Opening lines

"Firstly, check that your roof is fastened to the walls with hurricane straps."
questions.explain: Ordered advice with a transition: expository.

questions.topic: Section B: The Reflective or Expository Piece
questions.stem:
Opening lines

"Looking back, I realise our cistern saved us that September."
questions.explain: "Looking back, I realise" is classic reflective language.

questions.topic: Section B: The Reflective or Expository Piece
questions.stem:
It is a 2026 practice paper. The topic is natural disasters; the audience is homeowners. Make the planning decisions.

You must write a reflective OR expository piece of 200–250 words. Which plan fits?
options: A rap for teenagers about earthquakes.
A newspaper feature advising homeowners how to prepare their homes before hurricane season.

questions.topic: Section B: The Reflective or Expository Piece
questions.stem: Good. What is your purpose statement?
options: "To persuade homeowners in Barbados to secure their roofs and windows before June."

questions.topic: Section B: The Reflective or Expository Piece
questions.stem: You have 230 words planned. Which appeal will you build in deliberately?
options: No appeal; just list facts from the stimulus.
Kairos and logos: "With the season six weeks away, a set of straps costs far less than a new roof."

questions.topic: Section B: The Reflective or Expository Piece
questions.stem: For a 2027 expository piece aimed at parents, which opening BEST shows creativity and audience engagement?
options: "Tomorrow morning, when you pack your child's lunch, you will make a health decision that could last a lifetime."
"In this essay I will write about NCDs in children because it is the topic."
"Non-communicable diseases are diseases that are not communicable."
"Children de drink too much sweet drink an' dem parents ent care."

questions.topic: Section B: The Justification, the Notes Sheet and Exam Strategy
questions.stem: For a 2026 reflective journal entry by a homeowner, which justification is strongest?
options: "I wrote a journal because journals are personal. It is about hurricanes and it is for people."

"The purpose of this reflective entry is to persuade fellow homeowners to prepare early by sharing the cost of my own delay. The intended audience is homeowners in Barbados who, like me, tend to wait for an official warning. The context of communication is a community blog run by a district residents' association, read in the weeks before hurricane season, so I used a personal first-person voice and pathos to make the lesson feel real."
"My journal entry has imagery, a turning point and a conclusion, and it is well organised and interesting."
"The purpose is to inform. The audience is homeowners. The context is a blog."

questions.topic: Section B: The Justification, the Notes Sheet and Exam Strategy
questions.stem:
Jaheim is building his 2027 notes sheet (NCDs in children; parents). Sort each possible point.

Possible notes sheet points

NCD = not contagious; e.g. type 2 diabetes, hypertension
questions.explain: A key definition he can use in any form.

questions.topic: Section B: The Justification, the Notes Sheet and Exam Strategy
questions.stem:
Possible notes sheet points

Causes: daily sweet drinks; screens over outdoor play
questions.explain: Short, relevant and easy to expand.

questions.topic: Section B: The Justification, the Notes Sheet and Exam Strategy
